item.title: Microsoft outage means no email chimes or message pings, but still we stayed online
item.description:
An AP look at the global Microsoft 365 outage, which stretched into Friday the 13th and could reach as many as 450 million paid users, finds that people mostly stayed glued to their screens instead of going offline. Brands piled on with jokes — Burger King told whoever was fixing the outage to "take your time" and get a Whopper — while workers moved meetings to WhatsApp or turned to Xbox. One Redditor said the quiet office felt like a social event and asked, "Is this what the 90s felt like?"

item.title: Microsoft Outlook outage impacts users across US
item.description:
Microsoft Outlook went dark for nearly 17 hours starting Thursday morning, cutting email and chat for hundreds of thousands of users including in Utah after several servers became "unexpectedly unavailable." Down Detector logged more than 131,000 reports by 11:14 a.m., and Microsoft began returning servers to service that afternoon while shifting traffic to alternate routes. Early Friday the company reported "improvements in key scenarios" but warned intermittent outages could still occur.

item.title: Peru's Chiclayo welcomes its former shepherd home, and revels in pope's love
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV returned Friday to Chiclayo, the northern Peruvian diocese he led as bishop from 2014 until 2023, where organizers expected as many as a million people at his first big Mass in the country. Residents recalled his closeness to the poor through COVID-19, floods and a surge of Venezuelan migrants, and local shops sell "Papaletas" bearing his image. "Even though he's now Pope Leo XIV, he hasn't forgotten about his homeland," said poster vendor Rolando Antonio Mendoza.

item.title: US military downs 2 Iranian attack drones as Iran claims a strike on a US radar in Bahrain
item.description:
The U.S. military said Friday it shot down two Iranian attack drones headed toward Bahrain with no injuries or damage, rejecting a Revolutionary Guard claim that it had struck a U.S. early-warning radar there after a U.S. strike on a telecommunications pole in the Iranian port of Sirik. The Guard also said a liquefied petroleum gas tanker hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings, and neither claim could be independently verified. In Tehran, thousands joined funerals for the remains of 110 soldiers from the Iran-Iraq war, with services for 240 more held in other cities.

item.title: 'Our mission is to empower our youth': Latinos in Action to mark 25 years of operation
item.description:
Latinos in Action, the Orem-based program José Enriquez started as a Timpview High School class in 2000, is holding a 25th Anniversary Gala in Salt Lake City on Friday that is expected to draw about 400 students. It now offers more than 300 elective classes at over 250 schools, mostly in Utah and Florida, built around leadership, tutoring younger kids, service, college readiness and financial literacy. Enriquez, an immigrant from El Salvador, said he wanted to "create our own Latino heroes within our own system."

item.title: Microsoft struggles to restore email and other services in a global outage
item.description:
Microsoft said Friday it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress" as a global Microsoft 365 outage affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot entered its second day, though some users could still see intermittent access problems and delayed email. The company said it had no indication of malicious activity and was taking "a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure." In Britain, the disruption halted a trial in Manchester and left police forces unable to receive crime reports online.

item.title: US futures climb as Wall Street keeps an eye on Nvidia, Microsoft and producer prices
item.description:
U.S. stock futures edged higher Friday and Nvidia shares rose more than 2% before the open after falling 15% Thursday on news of Jensen Huang's resignation, with longtime CFO Colette Kress named interim CEO. Microsoft slipped 1.4% in premarket trading as its global outage continued, while investors awaited October producer price data after September's report showed the biggest increase since December 2022. Brent crude rose to $96.04 a barrel after President Donald Trump said the U.S. didn't "need a deal with Iran."

item.title: Why this Utah resort could be the state's biggest winner this winter
item.description:
Meteorologist Jennifer Broome named Brian Head one of the "snowiest adventure towns" for this winter in Outside Magazine, writing that it "is in a sweet spot for Super El Niño's elevated snow amounts." The Climate Prediction Center gives most of Utah equal chances for precipitation through February, but southern Utah has slightly better odds of above-average moisture, and its January–March outlook tilts wetter statewide. The forecast follows one of Utah's worst snow seasons on record, which produced the lowest snowpack since records began in 1930.

item.title: Darth Vader's light saber used in 'I am your father' duel sells for nearly $5 million
item.description:
The light saber Darth Vader used in the Cloud City duel of "The Empire Strikes Back," and also in "Return of the Jedi," sold for $4.875 million Thursday at Heritage Auctions' Ultimate Star Wars Auction in Dallas. Heritage says it is a world auction record for any "Star Wars" collectible, topping the $3.75 million it got in July for Luke Skywalker's light saber and severed-hand effects rig. The sale also offered 27 other light sabers and material from Episodes I through IX.

item.title: Provo GOP lawmaker holds narrow lead in tight Utah House race
item.description:
Rep. Lisa Shepherd, R-Provo, led Democrat Alan Jimenez by 228 votes in House District 61 as of late Thursday, with a winner due early next week once Utah County reports its last few thousand ballots. Shepherd blamed the tight race on a hard national climate for Republicans and backlash over the failed Amendment B, while Jimenez, a cybersecurity worker running for the first time, said voters feel ignored and see the Legislature as lacking transparency. The contest follows Democrat David Chappell's defeat of longtime Rep. Norm Thurston in House District 62, a breakthrough in a county with no Democratic legislator in several decades, amid statewide losses that cost House Republicans their supermajority for the first time in decades.

item.title: Protecting babies from RSV during the holiday season
item.description:
With holiday gatherings approaching, Carolyn Reynolds of Intermountain Children's Health says RSV cases in Utah are low for now but expects them to rise between Thanksgiving and Christmas, a concern because infants' immature immune systems struggle to fight off viruses and RSV is the leading cause of infant hospitalization nationwide. Protection is available through a maternal vaccine given at 32 to 36 weeks of pregnancy or an antibody shot for eligible newborns, and the 16,000 Utah babies protected in the 2024-2025 season were nine times less likely to be hospitalized. Reynolds urges parents not to pass babies around to people who may be sick, and most insurance covers the RSV shot, with free doses for uninsured families through Utah's Vaccines for Children program.

item.title: Intoxicated driver hit car with 7 juveniles inside, police say
item.description:
Six of seven juveniles riding in a Chevy Malibu were taken by ambulance to St. George Regional Hospital after the car was hit in Hurricane around 1:40 a.m. Oct. 24 by a Honda Civic that dispatchers said ran a red light at high speed; one suffered a ruptured spleen and five spinal fractures, and another a dislocated hip, according to a police booking affidavit. The Civic's driver, Victor Manuel Lomei, 21, of LaVerkin, was charged Thursday with DUI, reckless driving and several counts of negligently causing injury after police reported "an odor of an alcoholic beverage" and found an empty beer bottle. The affidavit says Lomei later claimed he believed he had fallen asleep at the wheel.

item.title: Firefighters with cancer have workers' compensation claims denied, despite Utah law
item.description:
West Jordan firefighter and paramedic Justin Young waited 111 days for Travelers Insurance to rule on his workers' compensation claim for recurring prostate cancer, only to be denied because the cancer was first found before Utah's expanded firefighter-cancer presumption took effect. Rep. Casey Snider, who sponsored that expansion, called the outcome "ludicrous" and said he has heard of 30 to 40 firefighters caught in the same gap, which he and Rep. Jordan Teuscher said lawmakers plan to fix next session. A new Firefighter Cancer Benefit Trust Fund meant to help during such delays has not paid out yet, and Young has begun treatment on his own health insurance.

item.title: Republicans score rare blue-to-red flip in Maine during midterm landslide
item.description:
Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage narrowly defeated Democratic state auditor Matt Dunlap for the open 2nd Congressional District seat, the only blue-to-red flip of the midterms not driven by redistricting; the AP's call came Thursday, once ranked choice tabulation finished. The rural, more conservative district, which Trump carried by 9 points two years ago, had been held by retiring moderate Democrat Jared Golden, while Democrats have flipped 44 seats nationally. LePage, who once described himself as "Donald Trump before Donald Trump became popular" but has also criticized Trump's tariffs on Canada, vowed to oppose whatever is "bad for Maine" once in Washington.

item.title: Arrest made in fatal Salt Lake City shooting
item.description:
Salt Lake City police arrested Ernesto Rosendo Flores, 24, originally from Las Vegas, on suspicion of murder and obstruction of justice in the Nov. 7 killing of Evan Cole, 32, who a witness said was shot near 475 W. 600 South after getting out of his truck and walking up to the driver's door of a white car that had pulled in behind him. Detectives tied Flores to the car through surveillance video and body camera footage from an earlier traffic stop, and cellphone data placed Flores in the area, the affidavit says. The white Audi A5 with Nevada "Raiders" plates and the suspected murder weapon have not been recovered, and police are seeking witnesses who saw it and a gray pickup heading north on I-15 that morning.

item.title: California man accused of human smuggling in southern Utah
item.description:
After his arrest in southern Utah, Hector Pec Tecum, 50, of Los Angeles, admitted charging passengers $300 each for a Nov. 10 drive from California to Denver, keeping what was left after fuel as profit, according to a police booking affidavit. Asked whether his riders were in the U.S. illegally, he said one had a visa but added, "I wouldn't be transporting them if they weren't illegal". The case, which brought three second-degree felony human smuggling charges in 5th District Court, followed a tip to a Washington County detective on a Homeland Security task force, and one person from an earlier immigration arrest told investigators he paid Pec Tecum $500 for a ride to Florida.

item.title: Colorado mom: Son's online game leads to missing Utah teen
item.description:
Colorado mom Khristina Tresp told KSL that her teenage son met a girl while playing Among Us shortly before Halloween and, after the chat moved to Discord, learned she was a runaway being held and hurt by an older man. Using a name the 17-year-old from Garden City supplied, Tresp searched county property records and sent her Zillow photos until she recognized the house, a turning point for a Utah teen who had been gone almost a year and a half. Adam Hunter Harmel now faces a federal charge of transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity, and court documents say Harmel may have enticed other minors and attempted to abduct at least one, leading law enforcement to seek information from victims nationwide.

item.title: 1,000 Thanksgiving meals for veterans in SLC, Ogden by Ken Garff employees
item.description:
Ken Garff employees are assembling 1,000 Thanksgiving bags, each with a frozen turkey, sides and a pumpkin pie, for veterans and active-duty service members, to be handed out first-come, first-served at drive-through events Friday morning at Salt Lake City's VA hospital and Ogden's VA clinic. Community and events coordinator Kate Terry said veterans now call ahead to ask whether the event is happening again, and that amid rising living costs "there's a huge need, and we're just trying to make a small dent in that" for people who sacrificed for the country. Those picking up a meal must show a military ID, a VA medical card or a Veterans Identification Card.

item.title: BLM rounds up hundreds of wild horses near Dugway
item.description:
The Bureau of Land Management is using a helicopter to drive wild horses into corrals this week near Dugway in the Cedar Mountain Herd Management Area, aiming to remove about 500 from a herd it estimates at roughly 660, well above the 200 to 400 the agency believes the land can sustain. Chad Hunter, head of the BLM's Utah wild horse and burro program, said he thinks it has been about four years since the last roundup there and that numbers double "about every 4 to 5 years"; removed horses go to corrals near Delta and Axtell for veterinary checks ahead of adoption or other placement. Jan Drake, who heads Wild Horses of the West and works with the BLM to dart mares with birth control, wants the horses kept on the range "in numbers that they can be healthy", though some advocacy groups consider roundups and sterilization cruel and have sued in the past to stop them.

item.title: Man charged in connection with 12 hour standoff in Yalecrest neighborhood
item.description:
Elliott Jones, 52, was charged Thursday with five second-degree felony counts of assaulting an officer and causing property damage over a Nov. 6 confrontation at his Yalecrest home that began after he called police about an eviction notice. Charges say Jones asked an officer whether he wanted a gunfight and pointed a hand shaped like a gun before four gunshots were heard after he went back inside, and that after a loudspeaker call-out he came out and threw an axe that hit the windshield of an armored Bearcat, causing about $10,000 in damage. Tear gas failed to end the roughly 12-hour standoff, and Unified police SWAT members eventually entered and arrested Jones Saturday morning, finding more than a half-dozen guns inside.

item.title: 'You can't land where we're at': Report sheds light on fire that killed 4 firefighters
item.description:
A 95-page federal investigation released Thursday into the June fire west of Grand Junction that killed firefighters Emily Barker, Nick Hutcherson, Sydney Watson and Nathan Matthews found that extreme weather and very low fuel moisture drove the blaze, while aging radios, network saturation, dispatch vacancies and trainees, and overlapping helicopter frequencies hampered coordination. The U.S. Wildland Fire Service and U.S. Forest Service concluded that the tragedy reflected "the cumulative effects of known limitations operating under extraordinary tempo and conditions". The report recounts Barker telling a helicopter not to land at the crew's site and, according to the surviving firefighter, offering her own shelter when the survivor struggled to close theirs.

item.title: Photographer's dream turns Great Salt Lake into high fashion while raising awareness for Utah's iconic lake
item.description:
Photographer Chris Carlson says a December 2024 dream about his Great Salt Lake photos becoming clothing led to a collaboration with fashion students at Utah State University and Salt Lake Community College, who turned 21 of his lake-themed concepts into handmade couture. The effort has brought in over $250,000 for Great Salt Lake Rising, organizers said, ahead of Saturday's runway show at This Is The Place Heritage Park. "My mission really is to keep Great Salt Lake in the cultural conversation," Carlson said.

item.title: 'Tour of Faiths' showcases diverse religious communities throughout Cache Valley
item.description:
Ten faiths that took part last year are opening their doors for the third Cache Valley Tour of Faiths, a two-week event sponsored by Cache Community Connections that begins Friday, with each congregation offering a 15-minute introduction followed by questions from visitors. Director Jason Tubbs, who says he approached 52 organizations, set one firm rule: "There's no sermonizing, there's no preaching and there's no proselytizing". Tubbs expects 25 to 50 visitors, and a separate Gratitude Concert featuring musicians of different faiths follows Nov. 22 in Hyde Park.

item.title: 'A force at KSL': Senior executive remembered after 2-year battle with breast cancer
item.description:
Tracie Palmer, a senior account executive who spent 14 years at KSL, died Oct. 19 after a nearly two-year fight with breast cancer, having kept working for 22 months after her diagnosis. Colleagues from senior business director Katie Gleed to KSL president David Pearce praised her kindness and devotion to clients, and in the words of senior major accounts executive Janet Aram, Palmer was "a force at KSL". Her husband, Matthew W. Lipscomb, asked that instead of sending flowers people take "someone special" out to a meal, and a celebration of life is set for Friday evening in Draper.

item.title: Zohran Mamdani has the most famous mustache in politics — for now
item.description:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani shaved off the trimmed beard that had become part of his signature look and debuted a standalone mustache while handing out water at the New York City Marathon, prompting The Cut to dub him "Mayor Mustache" and setting off online debate. CNN notes that mustaches remain rare among American politicians, with John Bolton long the best-known example in Washington. In a social media video, Mamdani said the look honors Movember, the men's health campaign, and pointed to a $4-million investment in a prostate cancer center at a Brooklyn hospital to show he was not just paying "lip service" to the cause.

item.title: Man twice convicted of minor exploitation accused again of enticing a minor
item.description:
Derek Thomas Horne, 43, previously convicted in 2009 and, in federal court, in 2018 for online offenses involving minors, was arrested Oct. 11 by Weber County deputies and charged with first-degree felony enticing a minor plus a sex offender registry violation. Prosecutors say Horne contacted an undercover Facebook profile posing as a 14-year-old girl and that his messages grew "increasingly explicit" despite repeated reminders of her age, and charges say he admitted using social media while knowing his federal probation barred it. Probation reports describe earlier lapses, including having his smartphone taken away in 2024 and "risky online behavior" on a monitored phone issued in 2025; Horne pleaded not guilty Oct. 20.

item.title: Rape charge refiled against former BYU Football player Parker Kingston
item.description:
Texts cited in new charges show former BYU wide receiver Parker Kingston, 22, telling a friend he "cracked her," which he later told investigators meant having sex, and the woman alleges she told him "no" four times before he had intercourse with her without consent in St. George. Kingston contends she never refused, though he says that an hour after leaving he got a text from her claiming she had refused. Washington County prosecutors refiled the first-degree felony rape charge Thursday, after 5th District Judge Jay Winward refused to delay a July trial and dismissed the case when prosecutors said the woman was not ready to testify.

item.title: Hegseth awards soldier who scolded him and his aides at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded the Joint Service Commendation Medal, which is not typically issued to junior enlisted troops, to Spc. Thomas Iglesias, the Old Guard soldier who reprimanded Hegseth's group when laughter was heard after the group posed for pictures at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier after the Veterans Day ceremony. Hegseth's social media post on the award ended, "Well done, Specialist." The episode came the day after Hegseth survived an impeachment push led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, an effort likely to be renewed once Democrats control Congress in January.

item.title: Ex-Weber School District custodian faces 6 years to life imprisonment for rape, sexual abuse
item.description:
Nolin Jeffery Maurer, 64, who had been head custodian at Eden's Snowcrest Junior High, was sentenced Monday to consecutive terms adding up to at least six years and as much as life after pleading guilty in September to rape, forcible sexual abuse and distribution of material harmful to a minor. A plea deal dropped four other counts, including object rape and forcible sodomy, and original charging documents place the abuse at a Pleasant View home and van, not on school property. The case began when the girl's father found journal entries and an unauthorized phone, and a forensic review of that phone turned up Snapchat and text exchanges that included requests for explicit images, according to the plea deal.

item.title: Officers, injured victims testify as man is ordered to stand trial for 4 deaths at WestFest
item.description:
A 3rd District judge ordered Matthiaz Centre Lauti Ioane-Register, now 18, to face trial on four aggravated murder counts and multiple felony firearm-discharge charges in the June 15, 2025, WestFest shooting at Centennial Park that killed an 8-month-old boy, a 41-year-old woman eight weeks pregnant and Hassan Lugundi, 18, whom a detective described as the intended target. West Valley City officer David Hagues testified that he ran toward the then-16-year-old as he kept firing, and two teens shot in the arm said they still occasionally feel pain after months of recovery. Another officer testified that while in custody at the scene, Ioane-Register said he "knew what he was shooting at" and "didn't shoot a baby."

item.title: Salt Lake man accused of killing roommate admits shooting was 'impulsive'
item.description:
Charging documents say James Stacey Riedman, 47, eventually conceded the Nov. 3 shooting of his new roommate, Kade Tuttle, 24, was "an impulsive thing" and acknowledged Tuttle "never made explicit threats of violence". Riedman, now charged with murder, had locked Tuttle out of their Salt Lake City apartment amid disputes over lights, food and items taken without permission, then fired once through the front door, according to the charges. Riedman initially told police he feared Tuttle would come in with others to hurt him, and he did not call for help after hearing a gurgling noise, the charges state.

item.title: Family mourns father killed in ATV accident, leaving 3 daughters without parents
item.description:
Hans Anderson's three daughters, who lost their mother eight years ago, are now without either parent after the 45-year-old died in an Oct. 31 side-by-side rollover on Strawberry Ridge above Hobble Creek Canyon. His sister, Janae Watson, said it was hard to accept that such a lifelong rider died this way, but she finds some comfort that it happened in the mountains he loved: "He died doing what he loved." The family has set up a GoFundMe for the daughters, the youngest of whom is 14.

item.title: Senators probing RFK Jr.'s testimony on Samoa trip after media documents refute it
item.description:
Democratic Sens. Ron Wyden and Angela Alsobrooks have opened an inquiry into whether Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health secretary, lied to Congress in saying his 2019 Samoa trip had "nothing to do with vaccines," after AP and Guardian reporting in August surfaced a letter he sent Samoa's prime minister that mentioned vaccine or vaccination eight times. Their letter to Children's Health Defense, the nonprofit known for anti-vaccine activism that Kennedy once chaired, seeks records on the trip, his 2024 campaign and his confirmation by Dec. 4. HHS has called claims based on the letters that Kennedy lied to Congress "outright defamatory", and while he was not under oath, knowingly giving false material testimony to Congress can still be a crime, though one rarely prosecuted.

item.title: US returns over $12 billion in oil proceeds to Venezuela since Maduro's ouster, report says
item.description:
A KPMG accounting released Thursday by the State Department says sales of Venezuelan crude, plus small amounts of gold, minerals and fertilizer, brought in $12.26 billion after Nicolás Maduro's ouster in January, and the Trump administration says nearly 99% has been returned to Venezuela. Under the energy deal with the interim authorities, proceeds go into a U.S.-managed account until Venezuelan officials win approval to use them for infrastructure and humanitarian needs; most moved through foreign exchange transactions with Venezuelan commercial banks, about $133 million went directly to services or supplies for the government, and approved payments included $5 million to law firm Greenberg Traurig. The report withholds the names of the 20 oil and gold buyers, though each was vetted for sanctions and money-laundering compliance, which the reporters call a sharp break from past practice.

item.title: US envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then head for Dublin to see Zelenskyy
item.description:
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner briefed Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin for about two hours after brokering two days of Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi that produced an agreement on a large prisoner swap but no major breakthrough, then flew to Dublin to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Kushner said the delegations "agreed on many of the principles," while Putin told the envoys that European troops in postwar Ukraine would be "absolutely unacceptable". Zelenskyy, who insisted Ukraine won't give up occupied territory for peace, also complained of new speed limits on the Starshield satellite service that he said a military investigation found were not random.

item.title: Google knows smart glasses have a privacy problem. Here's how it's trying to fix it
item.description:
Google's AI glasses built with Samsung, in frames from Warby Parker (from $395) and Gentle Monster (from $449), launch Dec. 10 with a tamper-resistant recording light, encrypted camera data and redaction of bystanders' faces in images sent to Gemini, though that blurring does not apply to ordinary photos and videos. Google's Juston Payne told CNN the company is researching more ways to warn bystanders as well as location-based limits, but said those measures remain in research and that a bare alert "can actually be weirdly disempowering" to the person being recorded. Privacy experts argue an LED is not enough protection, and Google's Shahram Izadi said the company has no plans to add facial recognition.

item.title: US Interior secretary visits Utah geothermal site, calls it example of 'energy dominance agenda'
item.description:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum toured Fervo's Cape geothermal station in Beaver County on Wednesday, calling it "a great example of President Trump's energy dominance agenda" and praising local support. The plant now generates about 33 megawatts for California customers, and Fervo plans to reach around 500 megawatts by 2028 and is in talks with Google about powering a possible hyperscale data center that could eventually push its output to some 8 gigawatts. Burgum said foreign influence has been behind efforts to turn communities against data centers, and he dismissed a ProPublica report that he stands to profit from the AI boom through his tech investments as "a complete false statement."

item.title: Families from France, US reunite in Veterans Day story 80 years in the making
item.description:
Richard Moseley of Kearns traveled to England and France to retrace the path of his father, 2nd Lt. Lonnie Moseley, a P-47 pilot who crashed under anti-aircraft fire in German-occupied France on July 4, 1944, and to meet the descendants of Lucien Lestang, the farmer who hid the wounded American in a barn for about six weeks. Lestang forged identity papers and passed the pilot off to German soldiers as a deaf mute farmhand, a risk Moseley said could have gotten the farmer's family and even the village executed. At the reunion, grandson Didier Lestang's home held a preserved piece of Lonnie's parachute, and Moseley said his father "called him his savior."

item.title: The historic SS United States is sunk after a long goodbye off Florida's coast
item.description:
The SS United States, the 1952 liner that was once the fastest ship afloat and is longer than the Titanic, was deliberately sunk Wednesday about 25 miles southwest of Destin, Florida, in a $13.5 million project to make it the world's largest artificial reef. The ship stayed visible for hours longer than organizers had predicted, which an Okaloosa County spokesperson attributed partly to crews flooding 128 fuel and lubricant tanks so it would settle evenly, before it tipped and went under around 9 p.m. "She is an amazing lady who will not lay down without a fight," said Coleen O'Malley, whose company handled the sinking, and the county, which aims to make the area the world's top spot for divers, expects the wreck to rest shallow enough for inexperienced divers to visit.

item.title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom as state's first Black US senator since Reconstruction
item.description:
Democrat Scott Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith after days of counting absentee and affidavit ballots, becoming Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction and the first new Democratic senator the state has chosen since 1947. The narrow result deepens what AP calls a decisive midterm rebuke of President Trump, with Colom drawing on strong Delta turnout, economic discontent and Hyde-Smith's missteps, including a beef-price remark he turned into an ad in which voters say they'd "pick another senator instead." Hyde-Smith, who had blocked Colom's 2022 nomination to the federal bench, conceded in a two-minute online video, saying "I respect the decision of Mississippi voters" and wishing Colom well.

item.title: For the first time, Utah Medicaid can help pay for Native American traditional healing
item.description:
Utah's Traditional Healing Demonstration has won federal approval, letting Medicaid help pay for certain traditional Native American healing services, which can range from sweat lodge ceremonies to talking circles, when provided through Indian Health Service, tribal or urban Indian health programs, making Utah one of six states with such approval. Matt Poss, executive director of the Urban Indian Center of Salt Lake, which revived its dormant sweat lodge about a year and a half ago with help from Ute healer Henry Howell, said the practices work alongside Western medicine, adding, "They all complement one another". Federal officials turned down Utah's request for a 100% federal match at urban Indian facilities, which will get the state's usual rate instead, and it has not been confirmed whether payments for the services have begun at the center.

item.title: Utah National Guard's Veterans Day concert brings together hundreds of student singers, veterans
item.description:
The Utah National Guard's 23rd Army Band and 480 Granite School District high school choir students performed for hundreds at the Tabernacle on Temple Square for the Guard's 71st annual Veterans Day Concert, which also honored students' award-winning essays about relatives who served. Gary Harter, a veteran who leads the Utah Department of Veterans and Military Affairs, tied the event to a long tradition of wartime music, from the Revolutionary War to Glenn Miller and Bing Crosby entertaining World War II troops. Seeing young people sing in tribute was especially meaningful, Harter said: "You like to think you did good while you were in the military as well."

item.title: CenturyLink is phasing out copper landlines in Utah
item.description:
As CenturyLink retires its copper landline network in Utah, a 50-year home customer and the owner of Salty Peaks Skate and Snowboard Shop say their lines went dead without adequate warning and their long-held phone numbers were lost, with owner Dennis Nazari calling it "a severe hit to the business". Parent company Lumen said both had been sent letters in advance and that numbers cannot be retrieved once service ends, though Nazari said the shop got its number back a day after KSL Investigators reached out to Lumen. CenturyLink shed much of its duty to keep copper lines running when lawmakers passed SB269 last year, after the Public Service Commission twice refused to release it as carrier of last resort, and Lumen plans to speed up the phaseout with notices starting next month.

item.title: Firefighters dig through rubble after NYC building collapse kills 2 and traps people in wreckage
item.description:
A three-story mixed-use building in Brooklyn's Flatbush section collapsed Wednesday afternoon into a neighboring lot being excavated for construction, leaving at least two dead and others buried under bricks and wood. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at least 10 people were hospitalized, four in critical condition, as about 250 firefighters dug by hand and with power saws and rescuers used dogs to find survivors, while FDNY chief of department John Esposito said "We do not know how many people were missing overall". FDNY officials said the search would go on for several days, and one resident told the New York Post that his wife and two young children, trapped in the rubble, were pulled out alive.

item.title: Man sentenced to prison for beating his roommate to death, seeks appeal
item.description:
Tyler James Vernon, convicted by a jury in November 2024 of murdering his 61-year-old roommate Steven Richard Nyce in a 2019 beating, was sentenced Oct. 15 to 15 years to life, with credit recommended for more than seven and a half years already served. The roughly two-year wait for sentencing stemmed partly from Vernon's unsuccessful bid to arrest the verdict, and Third District Judge Todd Shaughnessy later rejected a new-trial request too, writing that there was "ample admissible evidence" of the required mental state despite Vernon's drug use. Vernon appealed that ruling, and on Tuesday the Utah Supreme Court moved it to the Utah Court of Appeals.

item.title: Bipartisan coalition pushes for new oversight of license plate reader systems in Utah
item.description:
A bipartisan coalition that includes the Lehi-based Libertas Institute is working on legislation that would require warrants before police search automatic license plate reader databases in active criminal investigations, with exceptions for stolen-vehicle hot lists, missing persons and emergencies such as kidnappings. The coalition also wants independent third-party audits, which Libertas privacy analyst Emily Grimmius said the KSL Investigators' report this week shows are needed: a former Tooele County detective used the system to look up the car of a man whose estranged wife the detective was dating, misuse that no routine internal audit caught. "Internal checks are great, but as we've clearly identified through the story you broke, they're not enough," Grimmius said, noting more than 300 documented misuse cases nationally but none in Utah until KSL's story.

item.title: BYU students search for lost veterans decades later
item.description:
Scot Chipman's father, Marine A-6 pilot Jim Chipman, was killed over North Vietnam in December 1972, and his remains came home to American Fork in 2023 through the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency effort that BYU students now support with records research and relatives' DNA. BYU's Suzanne Adams, who directs its Center for Family History and Genealogy, urged families still searching to register as next of kin at dpaa.mil, and BYU reported its work most recently helped return two airmen, Lt. Blaine Wilcox and Lt. Edgar W. Nevois, who went down on a mission in Politz, Germany. Scot Chipman said the agency has the resources to keep looking: "So they're not giving up; there's always hope."

item.title: After surviving war, Utah veteran's new mission is helping others find a way forward
item.description:
After surviving eight roadside bomb blasts in Iraq and later losing a close friend and fellow soldier to suicide, retired Army Sgt. Josh Hansen and his wife, Melissa, founded Continue Mission in 2014, a Utah nonprofit offering free hiking, skiing, pickleball and other outings that let registered veterans connect with peers. VA data cited in the story put Utah's 2024 veteran suicide deaths at 65 and show that 62% of veterans who died by suicide that year had gone without VA health care in that year or the prior one, though the VA found Utah's higher unadjusted rate was not statistically significant once age was considered. Hansen, who stresses that recreation is no substitute for professional care, said "The reason our organization works is the networking," as introductions grow into friendships outside the group.

item.description:
Pop star Benson Boone, who lives in Utah, is set to play the opening intermission of the NHL Winter Classic, the Utah Mammoth's first outdoor game, set for New Year's Eve at Rice-Eccles Stadium, the league announced Wednesday. Boone, whose single Beautiful Things reached No. 2 on Billboard in 2024 and whose live shows often feature backflips, joins a holiday lineup that already includes a Post Malone co-headlined New Year's Eve festival at the Delta Center after the game. item.title: 'Dan the Man' one of thousands remembered on Veterans Day
item.description:
At the Utah Veterans Memorial Cemetery in Bluffdale on Veterans Day, Diane and her daughter Jennifer Underdown visited the grave of Daniel Lovan, the 26-year Air Force veteran the family called "Dan the Man." Diane said Lovan's drive to serve outlasted his military career: after a kidney cancer diagnosis he enrolled in every clinical trial he could, hoping what doctors learned would help others. item.title: New Ogden policy pinpoints when police may offer aid during immigration enforcement actions
item.description:
Ogden police unveiled an administrative order Tuesday, in effect since Oct. 19, that bars officers from asking people about their immigration status and spells out when they may assist federal immigration agents, after two late-summer ICE detentions involving Ogden officers were caught on video and drew backlash. Chief Jake Sube told the City Council that immigrants "do not have to fear calling us" and pleaded with crime victims to contact police, while Capt. Matthew Ward said such situations can be confusing for officers because they fall outside their everyday work. Mayor Ben Nadolski said there is "legitimate reason to be concerned" about how federal immigration policies are being carried out, and Councilwoman Alicia Washington thanked police for the policy while voicing concern about the Weber County Sheriff's Office's 287(g) agreement with ICE.

item.description:
Antonio Zarco-Orozco, 40, whom police first sought under the name Benigno Queredo-Centreros, was sentenced Monday to zero to five years in prison after pleading guilty to three third-degree felonies, including aggravated assault, and a misdemeanor for leaving a crash scene. According to charges, in July he pressed his forearm against his girlfriend's throat until she could not breathe, then fled in her truck after she had Siri call 911; the truck was clocked at 107 mph, and one matching its description hit a car before he ran off, likely swimming through Benson Marina to escape. Judge Spencer Walsh ordered the sentences to run concurrently with credit for 113 days served, and nine other charges were dismissed under the plea deal.

item.description:

Prosecutors allege Potter told UHP Col. Greg Holley he was home in Brigham City and would not come out to meet a trooper, yet Verizon records later showed his phone "actively pinging in the area of Tremonton". item.title: BYU-led study points to potential reason for mule deer population decline in the West
item.description:
A study led by Brigham Young University with the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources and conservation groups found that managing mule deer herds for a higher share of males is associated with poorer nutrition in females and slower population growth. Drawing on 15 years of productivity data and seven years of body-reserve measurements, researchers saw less fat on does in high male-ratio areas, which co-author Brock McMillan said may stem from food competition with larger bucks and from females being chased during the rut. McMillan called the result a "game changer" that "could partially explain the population decline of mule deer over the last 30 or 40 years throughout the West", while acknowledging the public and wildlife managers may be slow to accept it.

Third District Judge Theresa Welch sent Deon Jennings to prison for one to 15 years for the 2022 stabbing death of Willie Houston, 59, his aunt's boyfriend, turning down defense requests to lower the offense to a third-degree felony and impose five years of probation instead. Jurors had found Jennings guilty of murder but reduced the conviction to manslaughter after deciding prosecutors had not disproved that he believed he was acting in self-defense, and Houston's daughter Amber urged the court to show no leniency. Executive director Chantel Labrum expects attendance to climb this winter from about 250 to as many as 350 per meal. item.description:
Intermountain Health is rolling out a program called Safe Infant Sleep, with free consultations at Primary Children's campuses in Lehi and Salt Lake, where trained ambassadors tailor safe-sleep advice to each family's home and caregiver wellbeing is a central focus. A state health department report counted 137 sudden unexpected infant deaths in Utah from 2019 to 2023, roughly 27 a year. Of those deaths, Intermountain neonatal ICU medical director Jessica Davidson said, "About 93% of them were in an unsafe sleep environment", with many infants found on soft bedding, on surfaces not designed for sleep or on their stomachs.

item.title: There's 'pent-up demand' for skiing in Utah this winter. Will El Niño deliver?
item.description:
Utah skier visits fell 26% last season amid a record-low snowpack, though Ski Utah CEO Nathan Rafferty says the total still would have topped pre-pandemic records, and he isn't sure he has ever felt this much "pent-up demand for skiing" heading into a winter. Hopes rest partly on a super El Niño and on Utah's wettest July-through-October stretch since at least 1895, and KSL meteorologist Matt Johnson expects the active storm pattern to continue, though long-range forecasts reveal little yet about temperatures, a big factor in last year's shortfall. To ease possible crowding, Rafferty suggests smaller resorts such as Nordic Valley, Cherry Peak, Beaver Mountain or Snowland, some of which sell lift tickets for as little as $9.

item.title: Millions of Spaniards stage first general strike in 14 years as anger rages over housing
item.description:
Unions said 4 million Spanish workers joined Wednesday's general strike over the country's housing affordability crisis, the first since a 2012 walkout against austerity, with pickets braving storms less than three weeks before a Nov. 29 snap election. Spain is short about 750,000 homes, according to the central bank, and the Youth Council of Spain says average rent equals roughly 98.7% of a young person's monthly salary; "I'm 36 years old and I still can't move out on my own," said Jesus Gonzalez, who works in a Madrid hospital IT department. Angela de Miguel of business lobby CEOE called the strike counterproductive, BBVA Research's Miguel Cardoso estimated it could trim 0.1%-0.2% from annual GDP, and police reported 40 arrests by midday.

About 175 people crowded Sandy City Hall on Tuesday as the City Council heard two hours of comment on whether to spend leftover budget money on an environmental impact study of extending Highland Drive toward Draper through land that takes in Dimple Dell Regional Park. Councilwoman Kris Nicholl backs the study, saying she hopes it shows a bridge over the park isn't needed, while Mayor Monica Zoltanski opposes it, arguing the road would mainly benefit Utah County residents and that the $157,000 should go to public safety and road priorities instead. Many residents warned of added traffic and development, one urging the council to "Keep Dimple Dell wild" while a few argued growth demands planning, and a public hearing is set for Nov. 17.

item.description:

Father José Del Rosario, who worked closely with him during the pandemic, called him "a man who was very close to the people" and said Prevost had risked his own health. Greta Thunberg arrived Tuesday at the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, her first U.N. summit since Glasgow in 2021, saying host countries use the talks each year to "whitewash themselves" and warning that "everything and everyone we love is at stake." The summit follows a year of deadly heat waves and floods plus an energy shock from the Iran war, and co-hosts Turkey and Australia are promoting renewables while still leaning heavily on coal; Turkey wants electricity to supply 35% of global energy use by 2035, up from 23%. Her arrival excited many youth climate activists, and Amber Turner of the Alliance of Small Island States voiced hope that Thunberg's presence would remind people why they took up the cause; the talks run until Nov. 20.

item.title: Eisenkot unveils agenda to reverse Netanyahu's policies as Israel's new parliament is sworn in
item.description:
As Israel's new Knesset was sworn in Tuesday, Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief tasked with forming a government, vowed to undo many of Benjamin Netanyahu's policies, and his bloc filed bills for an official Oct. 7 inquiry, prime ministerial term limits and a reversal of the outgoing government's judicial changes. Netanyahu, who has made unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties stole the election, used a post-ceremony speech to cast Arab lawmakers as untrustworthy, prompting Eisenkot to call it "divisive" and "hate-filled" and cancel a planned meeting with Likud. Eisenkot has up to six weeks to build a coalition, while opponents who now hold a solid majority began moving to oust Netanyahu-backed speaker Amir Ohana in favor of Yashar's Matan Kahana, a vote that could come as early as this week.

item.title: New e-bike rules, speed limits being considered on all Salt Lake City trails
item.description:
Salt Lake City is weighing an ordinance that would keep Class 2 and Class 3 e-bikes off natural surface trails such as the foothills network unless posted otherwise, cap speeds on paved trails like the Jordan River Parkway and 9-Line at 15 mph for all bikes, and add yielding rules for e-bike riders, with first offenses drawing warnings. Public Lands Director Kim Shelley said complaints about speeding and inconsiderate riding drove the proposal, saying of one paved trail, "The 9-Line's just exploded," and adding that rangers would focus on education before issuing infractions. The city tentatively plans a Nov. 17 vote, following a state law passed this year that gave communities more authority over e-bikes and similar county limits in unincorporated areas.

item.title: 4 grizzly bears linked by DNA to deadly attack on mother and daughter in Canada
item.description:
British Columbia conservation officers said Tuesday that DNA conclusively matched a mother grizzly and three yearling cubs to the killings of Selah Reed, 20, and her mother, Jenny Balcarras, 48, near a trail outside remote Bella Coola, and all four bears were killed. Inspector Jeff Tyre said the attack "likely involved predatory behavior," which is very rare, and that the bears were not the ones behind last November's attack on about 20 students and teachers in the same area. The family raised the alarm when Reed missed her usual Saturday night call with her sister, and Nuxalk Nation chief councilor Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner said the killings have been "deeply re-triggering" for a community still recovering from last year.

item.title: Pope draws 1 million to Argentina youth vigil and urges them to follow model of saints
item.description:
At a Tuesday night vigil in Buenos Aires that the Vatican estimated drew 1 million people, Pope Leo XIV told young Argentines to reject the "idols of our time", among them money, drugs, pornography and success at any cost, and to follow the example of the saints. Earlier in Córdoba, after a Mass the Vatican put at 650,000 attendees, Leo met privately with 20 people including Alba Camargo, whose relatives disappeared under the 1976-1983 dictatorship and who called the meeting a "gesture showing that he sees us." Camargo hoped it would spur change as President Javier Milei's government slashes support for memorial sites and groups still searching for the disappeared.

item.title: FILMéxico film festival in Salt Lake featuring 7 acclaimed Mexican films
item.description:
Mexico's entry for best international film at the 2027 Academy Awards, En el Camino, is among the highlights of the Salt Lake Film Society's 15th FILMéxico festival, alongside films that played Berlin and Cannes. Organized with help from Artes de México en Utah and the Mexican Consulate, the seven-film series at Broadway Centre Cinemas opens Thursday with Los Hijos de la Costa and a question-and-answer session with its director, Bruno Bancalari, and closes Nov. 19 with a panel. Film society CEO Tori Baker said the festival unites audiences through stories that "celebrate Mexican culture, challenge perspectives and create meaningful connections."

item.title: Republicans pick new leader to replace Speaker Mike Johnson
item.description:
House Republicans picked Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio over Majority Leader Steve Scalise, 106 to 73, to lead them in the minority next year, with Speaker Mike Johnson sitting out the internal elections and Scalise's leadership run, which dates to 2014, coming to an end. Utah Rep. Blake Moore ran unopposed to keep his post as conference vice chair, though he said he would leave that post if he wins the top spot on the Budget Committee, a decision likely in December. Majority Whip Tom Emmer and conference chair Lisa McClain fended off challenges, and Rep. Brian Jack beat Rep. Rudy Yakym to lead the NRCC, succeeding Rep. Richard Hudson, who lost reelection.

item.title: Logan man given 15 years to life in prison for stabbing death of his father
item.description:
Clayton Robert Shaw, 35, was sentenced Oct. 28 to 15 years to life in state prison for the September 2024 murder of his 77-year-old father, Dennis Shaw, whose stabbed body was found near the Franklin Basin snowmobile parking lot in Logan Canyon. Investigators said the two had been feuding over an eviction notice, and police who stopped Clayton Shaw near his father's home found a double-edged knife that court documents called consistent with the wounds. After first pleading not guilty by reason of insanity, Shaw entered a "guilty but mentally ill" plea in January, and a defense bid to reduce the charge to manslaughter over his psychotic disorder was denied in August; he received credit for 760 days served.

item.title: Hidden for decades, a Bountiful veteran's letters tell story of Vietnam War
item.description:
About two years ago, Linda Cook found hundreds of handwritten letters and photos her late husband, Jim Cook of Bountiful, had sent home from Vietnam in 1967 and 1968, a chapter the quiet outdoorsman rarely talked about. Her son, writer Rick Mittelstaedt, helped her put them in order and found that a single letter could jump from asking about the fishing back home to a friendly-fire death, and the pair compiled them into a book, Love, Jim, named for how he signed off. The family plans to make it public and share copies with veterans around Veterans Day, and Linda Cook said that despite her husband's privacy, "it's a story that will help people" and he would like that.

item.title: Utah seeks diabetes patient experiences to support insulin pricing lawsuit
item.description:
Because the damages and restitution Utah can recover are tied in part to what residents actually went through, Division of Consumer Protection director Daniel Larsen is asking people with diabetes to describe how high insulin prices affected them. The submissions, treated as official complaints, will support the state's 2023 lawsuit accusing major drugmakers and pharmacy benefit managers of working together to raise prices "by 1000% or more in some cases," which Larsen said pushed some of Utah's 200,000 diabetics into choices like rationing. The state also wants the case to end what it describes as predatory pricing.

item.title: Beaver man accused of harassing family charged with hate crime
item.description:
Prosecutors charged Heath Loren Franklin, 56, of Beaver with stalking with a weapon, aggravated assault, child abuse and assault, each carrying a victim-targeting enhancement, over alleged harassment of the family living upstairs from his basement apartment. Doorbell camera footage allegedly shows him knocking a phone from a child's hand, hurling a rock at the child's toy car and, in a second video, yelling racial slurs toward the family's front door. In a separate case, a Nov. 9 traffic stop allegedly turned up nunchucks and a bat with a strap bolted to it, and searches later found a rifle, a shotgun, knives and brass knuckles, leading to eight weapons counts against Franklin, a convicted felon.

item.title: House Republicans quash effort to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth
item.description:
The House on Tuesday turned aside Rep. Thomas Massie's resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, as most Republicans stood by him after President Donald Trump signaled strong support, though Democrats taking over both chambers in January could revive the push. Massie's eight counts center on the Iran war, which he says has run 256 days without congressional authorization, along with reported cuts to a Pentagon office focused on civilian harm, the attempt to punish Sen. Mark Kelly and strikes on alleged drug boats. Hegseth, in his first Pentagon news conference in six months, dismissed the charges as policy disagreements and said of the effort, "This is sabotage."

item.title: 'I'm not that little girl teenager I was,' woman convicted in fatal crash tells parole board
item.description:
Eastyn K. Tueller, now 22, told Utah's parole board at her first hearing Tuesday that prison has taught her accountability and that she is "not that little girl teenager I was". At 19, after what she said was half a case of beer, she was going 98 mph where the limit was 35 when she ran a red light and hit a Ford Escape on Dec. 26, 2022, killing 61-year-old Rose Elena Mendez-Leyva; she pleaded guilty in 2024 to two negligent-operation counts and received 1 to 15 years. Pressed by board member Dan Bokovoy, she struggled to explain her speed, and she said she hopes after release to show students her injuries and warn them against drinking and driving.

item.title: Salt Lake City rezoned Smith's Ballpark. What happens next?
item.description:
With new zoning approved and the stadium transferred to the city's Community Reinvestment Agency, Salt Lake City officials say Smith's Ballpark is headed for partial demolition, possibly not until 2028, with part of the structure kept as a future event venue. Mayor Erin Mendenhall told a Ballpark Action Team town hall that "it is execution" now rather than planning, while agency director Danny Walz cautioned that a slow construction market, funding gaps and an ongoing feasibility study will shape how fast housing, businesses, open space, a fire station and a library fill the site. The first request for development proposals, covering the old parking lot, could come in 2027, and the city plans to seek an opportunity zone designation and is weighing a naming-rights rebrand.

item.title: Senate Republicans vote to keep Thune as leader after steep election losses
item.description:
Senate Republicans kept South Dakota's John Thune as their leader on Tuesday after three separate meetings in which members aired frustration over midterm losses of at least seven seats and their majority, with two more races in Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled. Wisconsin's Ron Johnson, who had circulated a letter seeking a delay, walked out as voting began, and Missouri's Josh Hawley said, "If you don't think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don't know what planet you're on". Thune ran unopposed in the secret ballot, and Oklahoma's Jim Lankford cited "widespread support" for him, while some senators pushed him to keep the chamber in session around the clock to pass war spending and other priorities before Republicans lose control.

item.title: Alleged spy plot targeting CEO Jensen Huang raises questions about Nvidia's future
item.description:
Probes into whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who had an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent, was targeted by a "foreign intelligence effort" have raised doubts about the future of the more than $4 trillion chipmaker, whose shares fell over 4% Monday and kept sliding Tuesday. President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating but that he believes Huang's account, and Nvidia's board launched its own inquiry while saying it saw no reason to believe secrets or national security were compromised; a shareholder has also sued, alleging investors were misled. Analysts note there is no clear successor, with Harvard's David Yoffie calling the board's position one with "almost no good options" and Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld putting Huang's chances of staying at roughly even and falling.

item.title: Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio elected to lead House Republicans in the minority
item.description:
House Republicans chose Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio as their leader for the next Congress, picking him over Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana by a 106-73 secret-ballot vote as the party heads into the minority after heavy election losses. Jordan, a Freedom Caucus co-founder, pitched himself as ready to counter coming Democratic investigations of the Trump administration, saying "I am battle-tested on the oversight front", while Scalise touted his legislative record and $67.9 million in midterm fundraising. The rematch follows their 2023 contest for the speaker nomination, which ultimately went to Mike Johnson, who is leaving the leadership.

item.title: Outdoor event venue to be built at The Point development
item.description:
The Point's board voted unanimously Tuesday to approve a 10-year lease and development agreement with Blackwall Ventures for an outdoor events venue on nearly 40 acres at the south end of the former Utah State Prison site in Draper. Blackwall partner Daniel Reeve projected $3.9 billion in economic impact and said the bond would be repaid through a venue fee rather than taxes, and the developer's website pitches capacity for "over 75,000 attendees at any given time," though July meeting documents put typical events at 30,000 to 50,000 people and Reeve said parking will cap crowd size. Board co-chair Jordan Teuscher called it an "amazing opportunity" that could draw people to the development's other retail, dining and housing areas.

item.title: Save the lake? Ben Abbott is focused on sounding the alarm
item.description:
BYU ecology professor and Grow the Flow executive director Ben Abbott makes himself available to almost anyone asking about the Great Salt Lake, warning that losing it could bring health-damaging dust, hotter temperatures, and the collapse of a brine shrimp industry and a stopover for 12 million migratory birds. He points to Iran's Lake Urmia, which dried up within 12 years after its rivers were diverted, and says Utah must "live within our water means," which the column puts at a 40% cut in use for a lake now about 30% full. Citing a state goal tied to the 2034 Olympics, at least $1 billion in federal money and philanthropic backing, Abbott predicts "Utah will be the first" to restore a saline lake.

item.title: Forum highlights debate over data centers, public input in Utah County
item.description:
A Monday forum at the Salem Community Center put developers, conservationists, academics and tech leaders on one panel to debate whether Utah County can host data centers responsibly, as Speak Up Utah seeks roughly 7,000 signatures for a referendum to overturn Spanish Fork's newly approved data center ordinance. Volition CEO Jeff Chavez said his project, now moved across I-15 from its original site near Spanish Fork Canyon, draws no grid power, wastes no water and seeks no incentives, while Grow the Flow's Ben Abbott argued every data center should be required to run on clean energy because "We can't sacrifice our air quality". Silicon Slopes CEO Clint Betts pressed leaders to explain the local payoff, saying the beneficiaries are big AI and tech firms and the Department of War and asking, "Why do we need them?"

item.title: A 'huge mistake': MIDA should not decide new data centers, House speaker says
item.description:
Utah House Speaker Mike Schultz told a Deseret News/KSL editorial board that letting the Military Installation Development Authority handle data centers was a mistake, saying "MIDA should never be doing data centers" after the uproar over Kevin O'Leary's Stratos Project in Box Elder County. Schultz said the public raised legitimate concerns about the project but the approval process broke down, and he wants a system in which the state sets high-level coordination priorities while locally elected officials decide whether to accept a facility. Senate President-elect Evan Vickers agreed the choice should ultimately be local, and both men said data center reform may be a priority in a 2027 session reshaped by elections, including MIDA board chair Stuart Adams' primary loss.

item.title: License plate reader misuse uncovered by KSL raises questions about oversight in Utah
item.description:
A KSL Investigators survey of more than 30 Utah law enforcement agencies turned up what appears to be the state's first publicly known license plate reader misuse: records show a former Tooele County Sheriff's Office detective used a closed case number in November 2025 to run the vehicle of the estranged husband of a woman he was dating, and his certification was suspended for 18 months. That search wasn't caught by a routine audit, and among the 23 agencies that responded, safeguards vary widely, with data kept anywhere from seven days to nine months and audit schedules ranging from weekly to none in 2025 at Clearfield. Clark Dice of the nonprofit Utah Civic Compact, which wants uniform statewide guardrails, said such audits "should be done by a third party" rather than internally, while Ogden police Capt. Matthew Ward said police want any new law to be well thought out and not "a knee-jerk reaction".

item.title: Judge's ruling could clear the way for Lindsay Clancy to be tried again in the deaths of her 3 kids
item.description:
A Massachusetts judge on Monday declined to throw out the murder charges Lindsay Clancy faces, which could let prosecutors retry her next year in the 2023 deaths of her three young children after her September trial ended with a deadlocked jury. Clancy's lawyers argued Judge William Sullivan should have removed the lone juror who favored conviction and let deliberations continue, but Sullivan wrote that probing the jury's deliberations would "improperly intrude" on its function and that the foreperson's notes about the holdout weren't reliable evidence the juror was refusing to follow the law. Prosecutors, who say Clancy acted deliberately while her defense cites postpartum psychosis, intend to retry her but haven't decided whether to pursue the same charges, and Sullivan also denied their request for a gag order.

item.title: Maverik Nitro Card saved a Utah couple at the pump; then came the fees
item.description:
A Heber City couple who paid what they owed for their motorhome's diesel were still sent to collections and told to pay $95 in penalty fees after their Maverik Nitro Card stopped drawing from their credit union account during a September road trip, even though the credit union said the account was open and funded. Mike and Kathy Bergin said TeleCheck, which processes Nitro Card payments, also reported the debt to credit bureaus, and their protests to both companies went nowhere until Get Gephardt reached out, after which the fees were waived and collections called off. Why the payments failed remains unclear, though a failed bank withdrawal can take several business days to surface, and a Maverik spokesperson wrote that the company is "committed to making things right."

item.title: California voters reject measure to tax the wealth of billionaires
item.description:
California voters rejected Proposition 40, a first-in-the-nation one-time 5% tax on residents worth more than $1 billion that its union backers said would help replace an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare funding the state stands to lose over five years, the AP determined Monday. The opposition raised roughly 10 times as much as supporters, with Google co-founder Sergey Brin supplying nearly a third of the more than $333 million collected by the anti-tax committee Building a Better California, and traditional Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association joined Gov. Gavin Newsom in opposing it. The AP Voter Poll indicates most voters under 30 backed the measure, while roughly 7 in 10 voters 65 and older said they voted no.

item.title: Investigators recover cockpit voice recorder from fatal Learjet crash site
item.description:
NTSB investigators have recovered the cockpit voice recorder from the site where a Learjet crashed onto a busy Palm Beach County roadway on Nov. 1, killing all nine people aboard, and the device is being evaluated at the agency's Washington lab to see whether it works and captured any audio. Pieces of the jet's left elevator turned up 1.3 to 3.8 miles away, showing the part broke off before impact, though it's not yet clear whether that caused the dive; investigators are also examining scattered storms and a pilot's report of manageable icing shortly before the plane plummeted. NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy again asked anyone holding debris to contact the agency, saying recovering all wreckage is "critical to the investigation" and to finding the cause; a preliminary report is expected in about a month, while pinning down a probable cause will take one to two years.

item.title: Utah restaurant operator giving away 10,000 meals to military veterans to say thanks
item.description:
Taqueria 27, which runs five Salt Lake-area restaurants, is giving free taco meals to those in the military throughout November and is prepared to serve 10,000 meals in all, at a potential cost of around $100,000. About 50 to 70 people a day have taken up the offer since it began Nov. 1, and operators expect the effort to pick up around Veterans Day. Owner Laxman Paudyal, a U.S. Army veteran who came to the U.S. from Nepal in 2002, is out of the country, and Biplove Timilsina, who manages the restaurants for him, said the idea was to "serve the people that serve us" for the whole month rather than a single holiday.

item.description:
In a letter Sunday to Senate President-elect Evan Vickers, attorney Ryan McConnell asked Senate leaders to set aside a Parsons Behle & Latimer report finding that Sen. Kathleen Riebe probably broke state workplace harassment and discrimination policies, calling the investigation "unreliable" and one-sided. item.title: Spring frost, dry summer lead to below-normal honey harvest in northern Utah
item.description:
Northern Utah beekeepers probably produced only about 65 to 70% of a normal year's honey, according to Jeremiah Johnson of Cox's Honey and Miss Bee Haven Apiary, who blamed spring frost, a dry summer and beekeepers losing access to public lands. Johnson said new medications for mites and other diseases are helping colonies build back up, although colony collapse remains a major worry in the industry. The bees are now being trucked to California to pollinate almond and other orchards, which Johnson said makes them "the original snowbirds" before hoping, like farmers, for a strong winter snowpack.

item.title: Officer killed, 3 officers and bystander wounded in Denver-area bus shootout
item.description:
Lakewood police officer Nick Graham, 33, a decorated member of the force since 2019, was killed in a shootout on a Regional Transportation District bus in the Denver suburb in which three more officers and a bystander were hurt and the gunman died. Police had been called about a suspicious person, possibly linked to an earlier hit-and-run, trying to board the bus, and a driver stopped nearby estimated about 20 shots and said "bullets were flying everywhere." Graham, who came from a police family, had handled 322 cases, the biggest caseload on the department's major crimes team, and one of the wounded officers remained hospitalized.

item.title: 5 states in Colorado River Basin elect new governors. Will it impact negotiations?
item.description:
New governors were elected last week in five of the seven Colorado River Basin states, but Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, the only basin governor not on the ballot, said Monday he doesn't expect major changes in the stalled water talks, though the turnover "does give us an opportunity to build new relationships," as he put it at his monthly briefing. With no interstate deal, the Bureau of Reclamation's own plan for managing Lake Powell and Lake Mead after 2026 is set to take effect in January, requiring Arizona, California and Nevada to cut 1.25 million acre-feet a year for two years while Upper Basin states like Utah may voluntarily trim up to 200,000 acre-feet. Nevada and Arizona are suing over the federal plan, and Cox said there have been no updates on negotiations as Utah prepares to host a seminar for new governors next week.

item.title: Run, fly, repeat: A Utah woman prepares for 7 marathons in 7 days on 7 continents
item.description:
Draper runner Melissa Walker, 50, is preparing for The Great World Race, in which about 60 runners hop between continents on a chartered plane to run seven marathons in seven days, eating and sleeping aboard between races at a cost of about $55,200 per runner. Walker had decided to "retire" from racing after her 26th marathon in 2024, but a 2025 half marathon rekindled her love of running with others, and she built up to 80 to 100 miles a week; signing up was "the only time I've actually ever been scared to sign up for something," she said. A finish in Miami, where her husband Paul plans to meet her, would bring her total to 34 marathons.

item.title: Utah House Democrats' wins come with mixed feelings over loss of some moderate Republicans
item.description:
Democrat Ofa Matagi, who gave birth the week before Election Day, leads 16-year Republican Rep. Steve Eliason by nearly 12 points in House District 43 in preliminary results, part of a wave that has Democratic and unaffiliated candidates on track for 16 House seats and break the GOP supermajority for the first time in decades. Some Democrats find such wins bittersweet because Eliason and other trailing Republicans were seen as moderates; Salt Lake County Mayor Jenny Wilson led a standing ovation for Eliason's homelessness and mental health work and said, "In my book, he's No. 1." Eliason, who plans to keep pushing his bills as a citizen lobbyist, attributed his likely loss to higher-level issues, while Matagi said she bears him no ill will but heard from many constituents who felt unheard.

item.title: Trump says FBI is looking at Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with Chinese agent
item.description:
President Donald Trump said Monday the FBI is examining Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a woman alleged to be a Chinese government agent, but predicted Huang would "be in good shape," adding that Huang told him he had no idea the woman was a spy. Huang has apologized in an open letter and pledged to cooperate, Nvidia has opened an independent investigation, and Democrats Sen. Mark Warner and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries want to look into it further, while China called the spy allegation a smear. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% Monday amid questions over whether China has been able to access the company's AI chips, which Huang has lobbied Washington to let it sell there.

item.title: FDA adds rare vision-loss warning to popular GLP-1 drugs
item.description:
About 6 in every 100,000 patients who took a GLP-1 for a year or more developed a rare optic-nerve condition in an FDA review of over 125 trials, versus fewer than 4 per 100,000 on placebo or other glucose-lowering drugs, and the agency announced Monday it will add a vision-loss warning to every drug in the class. The condition, non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, results from reduced blood flow to the optic nerve and can sometimes leave permanent vision loss, though the FDA says its underlying cause isn't understood. The dozen drugs affected include Ozempic, Wegovy, Zepbound and Mounjaro, and the FDA urged anyone with blurred vision, blind spots or distorted colors to contact a healthcare professional immediately.

item.title: Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky launches bid to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
item.description:
Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, with a resolution focused largely on the war in Iran that also cites military actions in Yemen and Venezuela; Massie said Hegseth "remains a threat to the Constitution." House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries backs the measure, so Massie would need only a few Republicans if most Democrats follow, but next steps are highly uncertain and Speaker Mike Johnson has tried to prevent the vote. Hegseth, who scheduled a rare Tuesday news conference on the threat, said his critics' disagreements "are with success," after The AP Voter Poll found about 6 in 10 voters thought military action against Iran was the wrong decision.

item.title: Jury trial for Tyler Robinson scheduled to last 105 days in summer 2028
item.description:
Fourth District Judge Tony Graf set Tyler Robinson's trial for allegedly shooting Charlie Kirk for summer 2028, reserving 105 days with jury selection starting June 21, 2028, after rejecting both the prosecutors' push for early 2028 and the defense's call for 2029. Graf said "unnecessary delay remains a serious concern" and cited other death penalty trials that began 21 to 43 months after charges were filed. The Kirk family called the timing "deeply disappointing," and Erika Kirk's attorney, Jeffrey Neiman, said a 2028 trial does not feel speedy to the family.

item.title: UDOT launches new quiz to help Utah drivers prepare for winter road conditions
item.description:
Traction restrictions in Big and Little Cottonwood canyons can take effect before a winter storm even arrives, and UDOT's new online quiz tells drivers which tires or traction devices their vehicle and route require. Cottonwood Heights Police Sgt. Lance Bess said officers inspecting cars in the canyons can simply wave through drivers who already carry a sticker from the inspection program UDOT has run for several years, while drivers whose vehicles don't qualify can ride UTA buses instead. UDOT traveler information director Becky Parker said the traction law "can be a bit confusing" and called the quiz a quick way to check before heading up the canyons.

item.title: University of Utah gets $35M to advance mental healthcare, research
item.description:
The Larry H. and Gail Miller Family Foundation gave $35 million to the University of Utah and Huntsman Mental Health Foundation to complete a 185,000-square-foot Translational Research Facility, which will carry the family's name when it opens in fall 2027. Greg Miller said the building will bring in experts from fields such as artificial intelligence, public policy and law to work with in-house researchers, and the university said the Utah arm of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study will be based there too. At the announcement, family member Sabrina Humphrey described severe anxiety and panic attacks that began about a year after her second child was born, saying she once thought people "could just think themselves out of" anxiety.

item.title: Gov. Cox says Great Salt Lake, housing, social media will be priorities in 2027
item.description:
Gov. Spencer Cox told reporters Monday that the Great Salt Lake, housing prices and social media's effects on kids will top his agenda for the 2027 legislative session, though he offered few specifics, and said a data center bill based on his executive order from last May is in the works. Cox said saving the lake is "still at the very top of the list" and expects newly elected Democrats to back the effort, while he wants Utah's $212 million share of an $18 billion Meta settlement spent in ways that benefit kids. He predicted the partisan shift could cost Republicans their veto-proof supermajority and may bring more collaboration with lawmakers, though the GOP still holds what he called "a pretty big majority".

item.title: Governor says Utah GOP leaders need to 'listen more' following election losses
item.description:
Gov. Spencer Cox said Monday he hadn't expected Republicans' "historic defeat" nationally to bring such heavy losses in Utah legislative races, where AP projections show the GOP losing its House supermajority, and he pushed back on blaming national sentiment alone, citing voter concerns about housing costs, data centers and trust in government. Cox predicted a changed session in January in which some bills he might once have vetoed probably won't be run at all, and said President Donald Trump "certainly shares blame" while hoping his administration reflects as Utah leaders are. He argued voters aren't embracing leftist policies so much as longing for normalcy, and said Republicans can win some seats back in two years only by being more thoughtful and listening more.

item.title: NASA launches $1M moon base challenge for students
item.description:
NASA's Moon Base Student Challenge, a $1 million multiphase competition announced Sunday at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex, asks teams of U.S. high school and college students to design pieces of a future lunar base in the moon's south polar region, with registration open through Jan. 25, 2027. Entrants will tackle areas from power and construction to life support, communications and astronaut safety, and NASA says no prior specialized engineering experience is required. Administrator Jared Isaacman told prospective entrants, "You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute."
