item.title: Utah singer 'very upset' with his latest performance on 'The Voice,' but he could still win the show
item.description:
Bluffdale singer Cade Mower, 35, is headed to the live shows of The Voice even though he was "very, very upset" with his Battle round duet, saying a lowered key and his own last-minute changes threw him off. Coach Riley Green advanced him anyway, and Mower, whose audition drew chair turns from all four coaches and more than 3 million YouTube views, now sees the live rounds as a "chance at redemption." Mower, who got his start playing Monday nights at his uncle's Murray bar, Club 48, also described turning the heartache of months of filming away from his two young children into being more present at home.

item.title: Utah Division of Outdoor Recreation seeks public input on southwest region plan
item.description:
People who live or recreate in Beaver, Iron, Garfield, Washington and Kane counties have until Nov. 30 to take an online survey shaping the Utah Division of Outdoor Recreation's long-range plan for the state's southwest region. The division says the plan will help set priorities for infrastructure spending through the Utah Outdoor Recreation Initiative and other state and federal funding programs. Respondents rank spending priorities, flag trails that need work and report problems they've run into, from litter and crowded trails to scarce campsites and unleashed pets.

item.title: How wet was Utah's October? The wettest in over 50 years
item.description:
Utah averaged 3.55 inches of precipitation in October, its wettest October in more than 50 years and third-wettest since 1895, according to preliminary federal data, with Kane County setting a record and valley soil-monitoring sites logging 488% of normal. The moisture, driven by hurricane remnants and other subtropical systems, caused some flooding, pushed fall mountain soil moisture to a record high and chipped away at drought, but statewide snowpack sits at just 70% of normal. Utah is on pace for one of its wettest falls and needs 1.51 inches this month to break the 1982 record, a mark that may already have fallen given early-November storms.

item.title: Mike Lee joins effort to delay GOP leadership elections after Democrats flip Senate
item.description:
Utah Sen. Mike Lee joined a letter led by Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson asking GOP leadership on Monday to postpone Senate Republican leadership elections until the party holds a postmortem on last week's elections, in which Democrats flipped control of both chambers. Lee said in a statement that Republicans shouldn't rush while two races remain unresolved, adding that "we need to pause long enough to develop a plan to move forward." The group hasn't openly challenged Majority Leader John Thune, who sources say still intends to run in the elections tentatively set for Tuesday, but the request signals internal restlessness after the party's losses.

item.title: UN climate summit kicks off in Turkey after a disastrous year of extreme weather
item.description:
The COP31 U.N. climate summit opened Monday in Antalya, Turkey, where Turkish Environment Minister and summit president Murat Kurum acknowledged the world will overshoot the 1.5-degree target and urged delegates to turn past pledges into action rather than set new ones. U.N. climate chief Simon Stiell framed the choice facing nations as "electric or shock" as the war in Iran, which has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, drives up fuel prices and spurs renewable investment. Developing countries are pressing rich nations over climate finance during the two-week talks, which the United States is again skipping.

item.title: Presbyterian church in Sandy to host interfaith Thanksgiving service
item.description:
Community of Grace Presbyterian Church in Sandy will hold its first interfaith Thanksgiving service on Nov. 15, inviting congregations including Congregation Kol Ami, the Utah Islamic Center and a Latter-day Saint stake, whose leaders plan to share scripture passages on gratitude, with music throughout the afternoon. Interim pastor Rev. Dr. Sue Coller, who did similar interfaith work for a decade in Lincoln, Nebraska, developed the idea with Jordan and Julie Clements, Latter-day Saints who attend the church monthly, and stake president Rob Yates. Coller called the event "just the beginning" and said she hopes another faith group might host next year in a space larger than the roughly 200-seat sanctuary.

item.title: A new poll shows Utah mirrors the nation on attitudes toward deportation
item.description:
A Deseret News/Hinckley Institute of Politics poll found half of Utahns favor deporting someone in the U.S. illegally even if they have committed no other crime, compared with 48% nationally, suggesting Utah's distinctiveness on immigration may be fading. Utah responses split sharply by party and gender, with 75% of Republican men backing such deportations versus 66% of Republican women and 38% of Democratic men versus 16% of Democratic women, while Latter-day Saint Utahns were 15 points more supportive than the national average. Notre Dame professor David Campbell said earlier findings of more moderate Latter-day Saint views predate immigration becoming central to the GOP, and that political views increasingly "shape how you interpret your own religion's doctrines".

item.title: Former NYPD officer and teacher's aide arrested in fatal stabbing of New York City jogger
item.description:
Sayed Mohassib, a New York City Department of Education teacher's aide who briefly worked as an NYPD officer in 2022, was arrested Saturday and charged with murder in the Oct. 30 death of Katie Suarez, who was stabbed in the neck while jogging on a Brooklyn waterfront path. The criminal complaint says surveillance video shows him walking toward the path beforehand and running away afterward, and prosecutors said he told police he went there with a knife because people were going to kill his family but denied stabbing anyone. The NYPD said supervisors observed "concerning behavior" around his denied January 2023 bid to rejoin the force, and local lawmakers are calling for an investigation into how he came to work in a public school, where the department has suspended him.

item.title: The vanity economy is taking over America's downtowns
item.description:
Nail salons, med spas, Pilates chains and other appearance-focused businesses are reshaping U.S. storefronts, with cosmetics, beauty service and fitness companies signing more than 1 in 4 retail leases this year, on pace for a record share, according to CoStar. Meyersohn ties the shift to e-commerce pushing stores toward services that can't be shipped, social media pressure to look good online and off, and younger consumers prioritizing self-improvement as milestones like homeownership feel out of reach, while cities and landlords have eased zoning and lease limits on gyms. New School historian Natalia Mehlman Petrzela described an "aesthetic creep" that now reaches straight men, and Tian Jiang, CEO of the 38-salon QQ Nails chain in New York, said such services have "become more ingrained in everybody's routines".

item.title: He went behind bars for Netflix. The biggest takeaway had nothing to do with prison
item.description:
Orangeville's Sonny Robertson was one of 30 participants, assigned as an inmate, in Netflix's reality-series revival of the 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment, filmed a year ago at a real Georgia prison with safeguards including psychological evaluations, round-the-clock medics and a safe word. Cut off from phones and outside news for two weeks, Robertson said the experience was "life-changing" and left him with lifelong friends, including his cellmate, and a new habit of meeting people in person instead of staying on his phone. Executive producer Jane Lipsitz said simply recreating the original study "would be unconscionable," though five participants dropped out over power struggles, mistreatment and conflict.

item.title: Trump says his deportation policy 'might have been too tough' for voters in the election
item.description:
In his first major interview since Republicans lost both chambers in the midterms, President Donald Trump told CBS's 60 Minutes his deportation policy contributed to the defeat, saying it "might be too tough" and that an immigration deal with the new Democratic majority is doable. He offered no specifics but floated letting some immigrants stay if they are working and, in some cases, paying taxes, even as he named immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller chief of staff shortly after the taping. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer mocked the move, writing "That's not a course correction. That's a promotion."

item.title: How 2 teenagers turned a haircut into a business
item.description:
Daniel Fuchs, who left school at 14 to apprentice as a barber and was licensed at 16, and vintage clothing seller Preston Byrd opened Duality Style Lounge in West Haven on Aug. 22, pairing a barbershop with vintage clothing shortly before both owners turned 19. Their partnership began after Fuchs saw Byrd on TikTok and, in his words, "just really hated his haircut," prompting him to invite Byrd in to make a video. The owners see the shop as a hub for other young entrepreneurs, and Fuchs said he wants to help young people build something "they can look back on" rather than chase money.

item.title: Hey, kids! Read 600 minutes, get cool stuff
item.description:
PBS Utah's Reading Marathon, which asks kids to read 600 minutes in November, has grown from a couple hundred Salt Lake Valley finishers in 1992 to 33,000 participants last year, long after national PBS stopped promoting it. This year's honor-system event ties into the Cox administration's Utah Reads Initiative and rewards finishers with an Adventure Pass of at least 30 free-entry coupons, from Hogle Zoo to Clark Planetarium. Station manager James Davie called it "the biggest thing we put on every year," while education manager Annie Frazier stressed that it isn't a competition.

Takashi Yamazaki's Godzilla Minus Zero, a sub-$20 million Toho production released near-simultaneously worldwide, opened to $31.6 million in North America, a record for a live-action foreign-language film excluding 2004's Passion of the Christ. It easily beat Warner Bros.' animated The Cat in the Hat, which drew a modest $20.5 million against an $86 million budget and poor reviews. India's Ramayana: Rise of a Legend also had the widest North American release ever for an Indian film, and Martin McDonagh's Wild Horse Nine posted a personal best for the director.

item.title: For nearly 1,000 years, the mesa in all its forms has been an American icon
item.description:
In a first-person essay, Dario Lopez-Mills traces the mesas of the American Southwest from their geology and Spanish name, meaning tables, to their role as natural fortifications and sacred landmarks for Native Americans, including the Hopi village of Old Oraibi, dating to 1150. Lopez-Mills notes how they shaped popular imagery through John Ford's Westerns and Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey, both using Monument Valley, and how Oppenheimer chose the Los Alamos mesa to gather scientists working to split the atom. Recalling a visit to the veterans' graves atop Acoma Pueblo, Lopez-Mills writes that the formations also "summon the pain of a people being torn from their land".

item.title: Beef boom pushes cattle past dairy as Idaho's top agricultural commodity in 2025
item.description:
Cattle and calves overtook dairy as Idaho's top farm commodity in 2025, ending a run dairy had held since 2003, with about $3.9 billion in cash receipts against dairy's more than $3.8 billion, according to USDA data. The University of Idaho credits most of the gain to "record beef cattle prices" and the high value of dairy-beef cross calves, even as the state's beef cow inventory fell 4% in 2024 and the national herd sits at a 75-year low. The university expects the shift to be short-lived, projecting that milk will reclaim the top spot in 2026 or 2027, while potatoes ranked third at an estimated $1.1 billion.

item.title: St. Paul's Episcopal Church already preparing for centennial celebration next year
item.description:
St. Paul's Episcopal Church, whose sanctuary at 900 East and 300 South was dedicated in November 1927, is re-lining stained glass with lead, repairing its roof and digging through its archives ahead of next year's centennial. Longtime archivist Russ Peck, who called the effort "a giant mess" for now, has turned up and framed the congregation's 1881 and 1927 charters while trying to identify boxes of old photos. The cruciform building still carries pieces of the congregation's original 1881 chapel near Main Street, including an altar, the bishop's chair and the original cornerstone, along with a plaque honoring the three New York sisters who helped fund it.

item.title: Floods bring rare relief to US Southwest reservoirs as Lake Powell rises 20 feet
item.description:
Late-October and early-November storms that flooded communities across the Southwest are giving a rare boost to reservoirs drained by megadrought, with Lake Powell rising more than 20 feet from its mid-September low, which University of Colorado hydrologist Martin Hoerling said dwarfs its gains from this year's snowmelt. Flagstaff's Upper Lake Mary has taken in more than 3 billion gallons since early October and Pagosa Springs, Colorado, has lifted water restrictions, but Powell is still just over a quarter full and the region remains in drought. Utah State University's Jack Schmidt said the Bureau of Reclamation is unlikely to change Lake Powell releases until snowpack peaks, typically around April, and Hoerling cautioned, "We need to figure out how to be resilient in a drier future."

item.title: Nvidia investigating reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence
item.description:
Nvidia's board said Sunday it is investigating reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, after The New York Times reported he had acknowledged being intimate with a business executive whom U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for Beijing. According to the Times, that executive, Alice Huang, a former Chinese TV reporter who is not related to him, is a top executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, which bought more than $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the past two years. The board said it has "no reason to believe" national security or company secrets were compromised, and Huang, 63, who apologized to the company for being unfaithful to his wife, will remain CEO during the inquiry.

item.title: Which movie most accurately depicts our AI-disrupted future? This US poll may surprise you
item.description:
A Deseret News/Hinckley Institute poll asking which movie will best capture life with AI put I, Robot first and The Terminator second among both Utah and national voters, though a plurality in each sample (24% of Utahns, 34% nationally) chose none of the listed films. University of Utah film professor Kenneth Collins said the options mostly asked people to pick "which nightmare or depressing scenario" seemed likeliest, and he read the large none-of-the-above share as a sign that hopeful AI stories "largely haven't been told yet." item.title: First-generation farmer in Parowan encourages other women to start farming
item.description:
Dayla Ulrich went back to school as her children reached high school, earning agriculture and sustainable food systems degrees, and has run Parowan's three-acre Sweet Pea Farm and Orchard for 12 years. After finding farmers markets unpredictable, she began inviting the community to Saturday French toast breakfasts on the farm, which grew into its main business and drew a FarmHER + RanchHER episode on RFD-TV. Ulrich, now teaching horticulture as an adjunct at Southern Utah University, says women have long fed their families this way and that feeding communities is "a really natural extension of that."

item.title: Advocates bring new food security network to rural Utah communities
item.description:
Chicanos por la Causa and Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla launched a "community-based food security network" Thursday in Wendover, where high school students packed 90 food boxes, with the long-term aim of reaching every county in Utah. "Many times Wendover gets left behind," program manager Leo Gonzalez said, and organizers are also prioritizing Salt Lake's west side and rural parts of Tooele, Summit, Carbon and Sanpete counties, with private donors funding the effort and local producers supplying food. Escamilla, pointing to 1 in 5 Utah children facing hunger and more expected safety-net cuts, said she is more hopeful about her food security bills now that Democrats are projected to gain legislative seats, including a third straight attempt to expand free school lunch.

item.title: Monarch butterflies get tiny trackers to help scientists follow their mysterious migration
item.description:
Scientists attached solar-powered radio tags to nearly 1,750 monarch butterflies this year, and about 175 tagged butterflies have been detected in Mexico so far, with early findings including the first evidence of a butterfly from Utah, west of the Rockies, joining eastern monarchs in central Mexico. The $200 tags weigh about as much as a drop of water, and UC Davis insect ecologist Louie Yang, who wasn't involved, called the technology "pretty remarkable" while noting it shows only which receiver detected a butterfly, not its exact location or whether it is still alive. The work comes as eastern monarch numbers have dropped more than 80% since the mid-1990s and western numbers about 95%, under pressure from pesticides, habitat loss and climate change.

item.title: Bicycle 'boycott ride' targeting Jewish-owned businesses in Philadelphia draws hundreds of counterprotesters
item.description:
A bicycle boycott ride by Philly Bike On Your Left, a self-described anti-Zionist group, targeting several Jewish-owned businesses in Philadelphia set off Sunday under a large police presence, with what appeared to be hundreds of counterprotesters waving Israeli flags and holding signs along the route the day before the 88th anniversary of Kristallnacht. Josh Shapiro's office said the ride was "designed to intimidate and drive Jewish businesses out of our communities", while the group said it chose the businesses over their owners' support for Israel and that its position had been "grossly misrepresented". The Philadelphia Democratic Socialists of America accused Shapiro and Mayor Cherelle Parker of conflating antisemitism with anti-Zionism, and the Anti-Defamation League's Philadelphia branch counted 106 antisemitic incidents in the city in 2025.

item.description:
Judge Rueben Renstrom on Thursday sentenced Ogden nightclub security guard Jeison Gomez Diaz to zero to five years in prison for manslaughter and co-worker Martin Esparza Espinoza to 364 days in jail, already served, plus two years of probation for negligent homicide in the February 2025 death of patron Albert Gutierrez. The guards fought with Gutierrez, who allegedly wouldn't pay for tacos, and left him in busy Washington Boulevard, where charging papers say a car struck him less than a minute later. A third guard, Jose Higinio Garcia Jimenez, received the same prison term last March after admitting in his plea statement, "I directed my co-workers to leave him in the street."

item.title: Caring for aging parents is getting more expensive
item.description:
A new AARP report finds family caregivers now spend an average of $11,508 a year out of pocket, nearly 60% more than five years ago and 31% of the average household's income. The burden falls hardest on households earning under $40,000, which spend an average 76% of income on care, while dementia caregivers average $15,846 and nearly two-thirds of working caregivers report job disruptions. AARP's Debra Whitman said the spending "can affect their own economic security," and the authors recommend tax credits, paid leave and expanded home care.

item.title: Hiding in plain sight? Russell Brand's conviction poses tough questions for UK entertainment industry
item.description:
Russell Brand's conviction in London for raping a young fan and sexually assaulting three women, with a lengthy sentence due Monday, has revived questions in Britain about how famous men evade accountability. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said she suspects abuse is still happening in the media industry, actress Sarah Solemani warned other abusers are "still hiding in plain sight", and the BBC reissued an apology over Brand's 2000s tenure there. Esella Hawkey, executive producer of a documentary on Brand, said television "does have a problem with dealing with that behavior and also in enabling people," adding that big names are hard to challenge because of their value to broadcasters.

item.title: 'The books moved feverishly': Santaquin residents move library books in book brigade
item.description:
Santaquin's library is leaving its 1901 building for a 12,000-square-foot space across the street, and 178 volunteers, including dozens of kids, formed a "book brigade" that passed 3,320 books between the buildings in two hours. Mayor Dan Olson said he found the library wing unfunded when he took office and finished it without a property tax increase, calling the library "a living educational center" rather than a thing of the past. More brigades are planned for the rest of the 28,000-item collection, with the new library expected to open in January.

item.title: The Bells at Temple Square to kick off the holiday music season
item.description:
The Bells at Temple Square, a 33-member bell choir, is rehearsing for its Ring Out With Joy concerts on Nov. 20 and 21 in the Salt Lake Tabernacle, considered the kickoff of the holiday music season. Because each ringer holds only certain notes of the melody, conductor Geoff Anderson describes the ensemble as a "trust exercise", and charter member Janine Scott-Silva said she manages about 15 bells and 10 chimes, often grabbing octaves without looking. With the heaviest bells weighing about 10 or 11 pounds, ringers warm up as if for a workout and usually play until age 50, which makes this Daniel Gibby's final season.

item.title: Why a new, soon-to-be colorful swarm of bees are coming to Salt Lake City
item.description:
A bee sculpture recently placed on Main Street is the first of seven in Bees Around The Block, a project conceived by artist and community organizer Landon Kraczek to showcase each Salt Lake City Council district's neighborhoods to the millions of visitors expected for next year's Salt Lake Temple open house. More than 400 residents have submitted design ideas, artists (preferably from each bee's district) will paint the sculptures at an event planned for early April, and planners have applied for a city grant to cover an additional $14,000 in painting costs. Lucas Horns of The Blocks Arts District said the broader goal is "a nice active Main Street" that guides visitors from Temple Square into the downtown core.

Zane C. Yazzie, 33, of Aneth, was sentenced Wednesday to 35 months in federal prison plus three years of probation after pleading guilty to three charges, including assaulting a federal officer, over several days of violence in March on the Navajo Nation. Prosecutors said he broke a woman's nose, strangled her and threatened her with a firearm, hit a second victim with a stick while he slept and later held a knife to his throat, then tried to punch Bureau of Indian Affairs officers who responded. item.title: Utah's only third-party lawmaker trails in bid for full term
item.description:
Forward Party Sen. Emily Buss, the Utah Legislature's only third-party member, trailed Republican gym owner Brooks Benson by 512 votes in the Senate District 11 race as of late Saturday, with provisional, overseas and some uncured ballots still to be processed. Benson told KSL it is "mathematically and statistically impossible" for him to lose and has already taken part in Senate majority leadership elections, though he hasn't declared victory, while Buss says the race isn't over until counting and curing are complete. If the result holds, the Legislature will have no third-party lawmakers next session but two unaffiliated ones, Sergio Sotelo and Patrick Belmont, whom Associated Press projections show winning House races, the first time in modern Utah political history that an independent candidate has won a general election race.

item.title: New leaders emerge at Utah Capitol after election shakeup
item.description:
Utah Senate Republicans chose Sen. Evan Vickers, R-Cedar City, as Senate president after Sen. Kirk Cullimore, who had been viewed as a favorite for the job, lost his reelection bid to Democrat Shana Anderson, and Vickers acknowledged after the vote that "the public has lost some trust." House Republicans, who gave up their two-thirds supermajority and about 16 seats according to current results, kept Mike Schultz as speaker; "We were not immune to what happened nationally," he said, calling for deeper conversations with Utahns. Senate Democrats kept Luz Escamilla as minority leader, while House Democrats are expected to pick their leaders Nov. 16.

item.title: US says it fired on commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman that attempted to breach blockade
item.description:
U.S. Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship that ignored multiple warnings and tried to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port, nearly a month after the last confirmed U.S. strike on a cargo vessel under the months-long naval blockade of Iran around the Strait of Hormuz. The disclosure follows at least two strikes the command did not announce, and it also stayed silent on Friday's limited strikes against an Iranian air defense system, which President Donald Trump confirmed and described as "minor." Separately, Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island and at the port of Jask, and Iran's military said two tankers had hit mines in the Hormuz area and caught fire.

item.title: Cloned, genetically enhanced dogs may soon be produced for military, law enforcement
item.description:
Warhound, a defense tech startup from Colossal Biosciences founder Ben Lamm and Anduril's Palmer Luckey, plans to produce cloned, genetically enhanced dogs for military and law enforcement work, reportedly backed by a $200 million seed round. The company pitches the program as a fix for dated breeding and training practices and for a reliance on Europe for more than 80% of military dogs, with the American Humane Society reportedly set to certify its training programs. Harvard veterinarian and bioethicist Lisa Moses told Scientific American that dog cloning is "still a fairly inefficient process" that requires many dogs "to have invasive things done to them and to be killed in order to produce one cloned puppy."

item.title: Orthodox Christian church in former Jewish synagogue prepares to build new church
item.description:
St. Peter and Paul's Orthodox Church, which worships in Salt Lake City's 1903 Congregation Montefiore synagogue, has outgrown the building, drawing more than 400 attendees on Sundays with what presiding priest Father Paul Truebenbach says are almost 200 more people looking to join. After a search of more than three years, the parish found a former Latter-day Saint meetinghouse in Kearns to use temporarily while it builds a church for 800 to 1,000 people on the attached lot, after which the downtown building would likely become Sunday-only. Inside the old synagogue, renovations added an iconostasis, a baptismal font and painted saints, and Truebenbach's advice to the curious is to "just come and see."

item.title: Israeli president taps opposition candidate to form government, in setback for Netanyahu
item.description:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Saturday gave opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief, the first chance to form a governing coalition after the Oct. 27 elections, moving him a step closer to ousting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's won a parliamentary majority, leaving Arab-led parties that made historic gains as potential kingmakers, though other members of Eisenkot's bloc have said they would reject a minority government propped up by their outside support. Netanyahu, who has made unsubstantiated claims that Arab parties "stole" the elections, called for a "national unity government" shortly before the announcement, and Eisenkot now has up to six weeks to assemble a coalition.

item.title: 2 men acquitted of murder after fatal shooting at Christmas party
item.description:
Jurors deliberated just under three hours before acquitting Zachary Gage Prescott, 25, and Kevin Charles Scarbourough, 39, of murder and felony discharge of a firearm in the Dec. 27, 2025, shooting death of Alex Powell outside a South Jordan home after a Christmas gathering, where multiple witnesses said Powell threw the first punch in a string of fights. Prescott, who fired the gun, testified, "I was scared for my life and I was scared for Kevin's life," and defense attorneys pointed to Powell's size and an alcohol level of .220. Prosecutor Samuel Sutton had argued the men "brought their gun to the fist fight" and killed an unarmed man without legal justification.

Fans packed the tailgate lots outside Rice-Eccles Stadium, some open since as early as 9 p.m. Friday, ahead of Saturday's 104th meeting between BYU and Utah, with Utah red dominating and BYU blue scattered throughout as both top-10 teams prepared to play. Utah alumnus Lo Lujan said BYU fans were welcome to join in despite "a little hazing here and there," while BYU alumnus Elias Pacheco said the prize is the right to brag "that you're the champ of Utah for the next 365 days," a title the Utes claimed with a 28-20 win in a rivalry dating to 1896.

item.title: With an ode to mate tea, pope urges faithful in Uruguay to build bridges of fraternity and faith
item.description:
On his only full day in Uruguay, Latin America's most secular country, Pope Leo XIV celebrated his first South American Mass in Paysandú before a Vatican-estimated 40,000 people, many from Argentina and Brazil, and held up the shared ritual of mate tea as a model of unity for passing on the faith. Visiting Casavalle, a Montevideo area beset by drug trafficking and gang violence where church groups build homes and support addicts in recovery, he lamented children who skip school "for fear of never returning home". About 100,000 people turned out that night for his vigil in and around Centenario Stadium, on a 12-day tour that had been in doubt after his Oct. 13 lung cancer surgery and continues to Argentina and Peru.

item.title: Utah veteran's post-traumatic stress reduced after magnetic treatment
item.description:
Retired Brig. Gen. Paul Peters, who served more than 30 years in the Army National Guard with five overseas deployments, says transcranial magnetic stimulation eased years of nightmares, anger and hypervigilance, and that the night after treatment he could "really, truly sleep for the first time" in years. The technique, FDA-approved for medication-resistant depression and OCD, pulses magnetic waves at targeted areas of the brain, and nurse practitioner Thomas Trevort of Optimal TMS said testing shows it can help regrow stress-damaged dendritic spines; newer protocols have shortened what he described as a traditional 36-day program to as little as one day-long session. Peters and Trevort, who also underwent the treatment, now want to spread the word to other veterans struggling with PTSD.

item.title: Polish gunman who killed 6 people in Krakow has 'ultranationalistic' views, authorities say
item.description:
In what Poland's defense minister called an "act of terror," a 25-year-old man drove to several spots in Krakow's Main Square on Saturday and opened fire with an automatic weapon at each stop, killing six people and injuring 15 before police shot and wounded him, authorities said. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the unnamed suspect holds "ultranationalistic" views, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the bodies of three of the man's close family members were later found in his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski. Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland, though a researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague said the attacker's gear and overall look were similar to those of other extreme-right lone actors in Europe.

item.title: Want to fly to the moon? NASA is looking for new astronauts to help grow its Artemis program
item.description:
NASA is taking applications through Dec. 3 for its 25th astronaut class, with final selections expected by late 2027 and training to begin by early 2028, the year the agency intends to return astronauts to the lunar surface. The agency has only 32 active astronauts, and "We have far more work than we have astronauts," Artemis III commander Randy Bresnik told the AP. Crewmate Frank Rubio, who holds the U.S. endurance record of 371 consecutive days in space, cautioned that the moon trip itself would be "about 1% of your experience" after two years of mandatory training and possibly several more years of waiting to fly.

item.title: Melania Trump and LSU announce a scholarship program for students who were in foster care

At an LSU event on the day she planned to attend the LSU-Alabama game, Trump said the effort would give those students "an anchor of stability," and said 14 scholars at LSU and nine at Alabama are among 100 students supported across 26 schools this semester. The program is an offshoot of her Be Best campaign, and LSU President Wade Rousse said "talent is everywhere but we understand that opportunity is not," calling access one of the university's highest priorities.

Scholarship tickets for students who qualify for free and reduced lunch cost $50 versus the $185 standard price and cover lift tickets, transportation, coaching and rentals, with partial scholarships for families earning under $120,000. In Texas, where President Donald Trump's push for five extra GOP seats started the fight, Republicans picked off only the 32nd District and lost Rep. Monica De La Cruz's seat, while California's retaliatory map flipped all five of its targets to Democrats. item.title: Scientists say they've found the strongest evidence yet of red blood cells in a dinosaur bone
item.description:
Researchers studying a 115 million-year-old leg bone from the theropod Aratasaurus museunacionali, dug up in northeastern Brazil, report in PNAS what they call the strongest evidence yet of fossilized red blood cells, including the first in situ detection of heme in a dinosaur fossil. Lead author Kliti Grice of Curtin University said the bigger point is that "we now have approaches that can be applied to other fossils" well beyond this one, though she cautioned against drawing conclusions about the animal's physiology from one specimen. Not everyone is convinced: North Carolina State's Mary Schweitzer said the findings don't meet established standards for identifying fossilized blood cells, while still calling the authors' multi-technique approach an exciting advance.

The action coincided with two days of "Stop Dirty Data Centres" events in 15 European countries, including smaller Friday protests near Berlin and outside the Polish parliament, as organizers seek a moratorium on large developments over social and environmental concerns. Rock art in the area, some dating to 3500 B.C. according to AllMoab.com, is protected by the Archaeological Resources Protection Act, and officials said damaged panels "cannot be restored to their original condition". Wilson said the goal is for students to feel valued, adding, "We're here to help each other."

item.title: Unsealed indictment shows political motives behind alleged obstruction by local sheriffs
item.description:
Newly unsealed, less-redacted indictments allege that Wasatch County Sheriff Jared Rigby, now on paid leave, sent an anonymous letter attacking the credibility of Summit County detective Eric Mainord, an investigator in the Kouri Richins case who was running against Rigby for sheriff. Prosecutors say the letter's 13 paragraphs matched a records request for Mainord's personnel file signed by retired Summit County Sheriff Dave Edmunds, and that Rigby hoped to use the trial's publicity to push the detective out of the race; Summit County Sheriff Kacey Bates told Rigby the effort "feels slimy." Rigby is also accused of sending a fake anonymous email urging Lt. Jeremy Hales not to run, and Hales went on to beat Rigby in the June primary and win this week's election.

item.title: Tesla set to wind down production of Cybertruck
item.description:
Tesla will begin winding down Cybertruck production at its Austin, Texas, plant, the only one that makes the truck, "around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," CEO Elon Musk posted Friday on X. It wasn't clear whether the truck would be built elsewhere, though lead engineer Wes Morrill wrote that it "lives on through Cybercab". The vehicle fell well short of Musk's 2023 estimate of 500,000 a year, with Tesla reporting fewer than 37,000 sales of all models other than the Model 3 and Model Y this year, and the news followed a drop of more than 12% in both Tesla and SpaceX shares over the first two days of trading after the midterms.

item.title: Cox issues state of emergency over flooding in southern Utah
item.description:
Gov. Spencer Cox declared a state of emergency Friday for San Juan and Washington counties, freeing state resources and opening the door to federal or interstate aid after weeks of flooding that the governor said "damaged homes, disrupted access to drinking water and cut off important travel routes". The National Weather Service reported the San Juan River near the Four Corners crested at 21.3 feet Tuesday, nearly 7 feet above its old record, while Gould Wash flooding in Hurricane affected roughly 130 homes or RVs and the Comb Wash Bridge on U.S. 163 was closed. A Climate Prediction Center meteorologist tied the subtropical storms to a strong El Niño, which has helped lift parts of Utah out of drought but also caused flooding.

item.title: Midvale gold heist leaves store with heavy losses
item.description:
Thieves backed a stolen truck through the glass entrance of Utah Gold Buyers in Midvale early Tuesday and took gold jewelry, coins and Cartier bracelets that owner Cole Cannon values at around $50,000, with repairs to his store and a neighboring business that he estimates could top $100,000. Cannon believes the break-in by at least three people was planned, though the ringleader who stayed longest went for a silver coin case instead of the gold jewelry: "He was basically stepping over gold to pick up silver." Unified police say the truck had been stolen about two hours earlier from a South Jordan home and was found abandoned in Sandy; no arrests have been announced.

item.title: Provo River Trail enters final phase of construction, expanding for safety and accessibility
item.description:
Provo has started the last piece of a trail overhaul it began in 2018, widening a 0.8-mile stretch of the Provo River Trail between Columbia Lane and University Parkway from 6 feet to 14 feet and adding a pedestrian bridge east of State Street. The $5 million project, mostly covered by a $4.6 million Mountainland Association of Governments grant, aims to fix sightlines, grades and sharp turns and meet ADA rules, and parks planning and project manager John Bunderson says public input treats the segment as "the keystone part of the project" that people want finished. Runner Mary Ann Nielsen, whose child was hit by an electric scooter on this section, welcomes the extra width, though trail closures are expected through July and construction through summer 2027.

item.title: Panda fans flock to Zoo Atlanta for the debut of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang
item.description:
Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, 6-year-old giant pandas on a 10-year loan from China, made their public debut Friday at Zoo Atlanta, whose enclosure had been empty since four pandas went back to China in 2024, ending a 25-year partnership amid strained relations. The AP notes China's long use of pandas in diplomacy, and Chinese Ambassador Xie Feng said the arrival "marks the renewal of a decade-long bond between China and Zoo Atlanta." Visitors included an 8-year-old from Sacramento who called seeing them "the best thing in my life" and a Georgia Tech student from the pandas' hometown of Chengdu, and Zoo Atlanta is now one of three U.S. zoos with the bears.

item.title: USU partnership with local zoo is a win-win for exotic animals, future veterinarians
item.description:
Utah State University veterinary students are getting hands-on practice with birds, reptiles, big cats and primates, from routine checkups to the occasional surgery, through a partnership with Logan's Zootah, formerly Willow Park Zoo. Dr. Mike McEntire, who teaches zoological medicine, says zoos struggle to find specialists, noting "There's only six of us in the whole state that have this kind of specialty," and that while a handful of vet schools partner with local zoos, to his knowledge none offer this early access. Zootah director Troy Cooper, who also teaches an exotic-animal elective, says the exposure could help the small zoo reach full accreditation.

item.title: San Juan County man given 16 years for possessing child sex abuse material
item.description:
Johnston Blackhorse, 43, of Aneth was sentenced Wednesday to 16 years in federal prison plus lifetime probation for receiving and possessing child sexual abuse material, years after calling himself "an untreatable pedophile" at a revocation hearing over obscene drawings of children. He was already on supervised release for a 2015 conviction when probation officers on a February 2025 home visit found a forensic wiping program that had been used that day on his computer, and a fuller examination recovered six images from deleted space. U.S. Attorney Melissa Holyoak said his pattern of behavior shows he "remains a dangerous offender with a significant likelihood of recidivism."

item.title: Utah women raise awareness about heart health through personal stories, quilting
item.description:
A group of local women has made more than 80 quilts to be auctioned at the Holiday Quilt Show, Nov. 10-12 at Thanksgiving Point, with proceeds going to Intermountain Health's Women's Heart and Vascular Program. Intermountain cardiac surgeon Dr. John Doty says medicine has historically focused on heart disease in men, and that women's warning signs can differ, with pain that may show up in the arm, neck or stomach. BYU nursing student Chloe Harmer, 21, who has had two open-heart surgeries, offers a simple message: "Don't take your health for granted and take care of your heart".

item.title: Why does BYU-Utah rivalry game trigger such deep emotions? Sports psychology prof weighs in
item.description:
A new Y2 Analytics poll of 786 Utahns found BYU narrowly ahead of Utah, 37% to 34%, as the team residents usually root for, though roughly 52% sided with the Utes when forced to choose, and 77% of BYU fans said they would likely cheer for Utah in a big out-of-state matchup compared with 47% of Utah fans returning the favor. University of Utah sports psychology professor Matt Moore traces the intensity to social identity, noting that rival fans share families, workplaces and church communities, which can make a loss or slight feel personal. Moore says social media amplifies a "loud minority" and urges fans to care deeply but remember "it is just a game."

item.title: Data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
item.description:
Democrats who flipped governorships in states including Texas, Ohio and Georgia wove hard lines against data centers into their platforms, and Data Center Watch found 32 of 34 winning governor candidates back stronger regulation or restrictions, with 12 supporting bans or moratoriums. Morgan Stanley singled out Gina Hinojosa's defeat of Texas Gov. Greg Abbott as the "most important election result" for data center development, while Redbud Consulting counted restrictions approved in 44 of 45 completed local referendums and the AP Voter Poll found about three-quarters of voters oppose a new data center in their community. OpenAI asked policymakers for "clear rules for how the industry builds", and the Data Center Coalition's Dan Diorio warned that moratoriums would carry real-world consequences such as lost local tax revenue.

item.title: Anthropic rapidly accelerating AI development amid slowdown calls, research group says
item.description:
An analysis by the Berkeley nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research, which Anthropic gave "unprecedented access to internal data" and staff interviews over about 11 weeks, estimates the company is improving its models on "well specified tasks" around twice as fast as a year earlier. METR ruled out growth in training compute and guessed the speedup comes from using AI itself to improve AI, while cautioning that it could be overstating its findings and that Anthropic's redactions limited the detail it could share. Co-founder Sam McCandlish said many of the conclusions matched his own, and the report lands as CEO Dario Amodei urges the industry to slow down and the company prepares what could be the biggest IPO ever.

item.title: Groundbreaking ceremony held in celebration of Davis County's replacement animal shelter
item.description:
Davis County broke ground in Fruit Heights on a 27,223-square-foot animal shelter to replace the county's only shelter, an 11,000-square-foot building from 1985 that lacks room to quarantine sick animals and no longer meets the standard of care. The new building will hold 60 dogs in larger, angled kennels meant to cut stress and noise, up to 94 cats and some exotic animals, plus its own veterinary clinic, a community room and a fenced exercise area. Construction is set to begin in January with an expected opening in mid-2028, and Davis County Animal Care director Michelle Hicks said the community "has deserved better for a little while".

item.title: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch may have so much plastic, it's changing the color of the ocean
item.description:
University of Bergen researchers, writing in Communications Earth & Environment, found that 20 years of satellite data show the Great Pacific Garbage Patch brightening in blue and green wavelengths relative to the surrounding ocean, likely shifting toward cyan, and their simulations pointed to microplastics rather than natural causes such as phytoplankton. Direct measurements at the patch are still needed to show the color "is directly and exclusively caused by plastics," said PhD candidate Shea Cheatham, but if confirmed, the approach could help track tiny particles that are otherwise laborious to quantify and that may help explain why so little of the plastic entering the ocean is found floating. Richard Thompson of the University of Plymouth, who was not involved, said remote detection from satellites would be faster and cheaper than counting debris piece by piece.

item.title: At 96, Utah woman continues making teddy bears for kids
item.description:
Volunteers with the Teddy Bear Project, which 96-year-old Ruth Brasher has helped lead for 33 years, have sewn, stuffed and decorated more than 23,000 bears for children visiting the Utah County Children's Justice Center, a child-friendly setting for kids involved in abuse investigations. Brasher said the comfort reaches beyond the children themselves, asking, "what about the mothers, fathers who see their child having an opportunity to overcome a difficult experience in their life?" Springville volunteer Dana Sorenson, who joined after meeting Brasher about a year ago, called the work "a beautiful way to use my talent" to make something of worth for young kids.

item.title: Betting is high stakes among young gamblers — even in a state where gambling is illegal
item.description:
Gambling is illegal in Utah, but phones make betting easy even for minors, and Caleb Silverman of the recovery app Bettrr said more than 2,200 Utahns called his gambling hotline last year, up 28%, while Common Sense Media found nearly half of boys have bet on sports by age 17. BYU professor Mark Johnson's research in states that legalized betting found investing fell as much as 20% among frequent bettors, with the biggest debt increases in the most vulnerable households, and he warns overconfident young bettors that "You're going to lose to the house 98% of the time." Required financial literacy classes, including one at Skyridge High School, now cover gambling, as Attorney General Derek Brown pursues criminal charges against prediction market company Kalshi and its executives, who have been ordered to appear in 3rd District Court next month.

item.title: 4 Ogden women among the wave of Democrats poised to flip seats in the Utah Legislature
item.description:
Weber County, which sent no Democrats to the Utah House last year, is poised to send three, with Rosemary Lesser, Kim James and Angela Choberka all on track to win Republican-held seats while CJ Hernandez leads Jill Koford for the open District 5 Senate seat. Statewide, at least 13 Democrats were on track to unseat GOP House incumbents and two unaffiliated candidates to beat other Republicans, which would shift the chamber from 61-14 to 46 Republicans, 27 Democrats and two unaffiliated members, while House Speaker Mike Schultz said, "There are lessons from this election at every level". James said many lifelong Republicans told her while canvassing that they couldn't stand it anymore, often naming President Trump, and Hernandez and Lesser said voters raised corruption, data centers, rising costs and the Great Salt Lake.

item.title: Whitney Leavitt's life beyond 'Secret Lives' is coming to Hulu
item.description:
Hulu has greenlit an untitled reality series about Whitney Leavitt, who announced her exit from The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives in May after five seasons; she will executive produce it with her husband, Connor, through Leavitt Media House, with Jeff Jenkins Productions also producing. Leavitt marked the news Wednesday with an Instagram video of fans' speculation and the caption "See you soon." The show adds to a busy stretch that has included a Dancing With the Stars semifinal finish and a record-setting Broadway run in Chicago, with a December return to Broadway in Just In Time and a film debut in Netflix's All For Christmas still ahead.

item.title: Corrections department disputes claims of inadequate inmate care during month-long lockdown
item.description:
Utah Corrections Watch founder Nadine Salyer says inmates told her of days without leaving their cells or showering, refunded commissary orders, missed medications and even "three different people swallowing razor blades" during the monthlong lockdown at the Salt Lake City and Gunnison prisons, but deputy corrections commissioner Mike Schoenfeld says those claims are false and that the department has "zero reports of that stuff." Schoenfeld acknowledged that visitation, programming and education were disrupted and that commissary was affected for about a week, but he said inmates still got an hour out of their cells each day. The lockdown followed a Sept. 24 attack at the Central Utah Correctional Facility that nearly killed a sergeant, which Schoenfeld called a coordinated effort by a group planning further attacks; officers now work in pairs, and the last tiers reopened Oct. 29.

item.title: Man gets probation for threatening family of man involved in Stratos data center project
item.description:
Casey Hill, a spokesman for Kevin O'Leary on the Stratos data center project in Box Elder County, told a judge Thursday that "There is a fundamental difference between opposing a project and threatening the lives of the people that are involved," as Daniel Charles Kasimow, 56, was sentenced to two years of probation for misdemeanor stalking. Charges say Kasimow kept texting threats in late May, including that Hill and a business partner would be dead if the data center came to Utah, and that Hill spent thousands on security and relocated while his daughter was in hospice care. Under a plea deal, eight lesser counts were dismissed and Judge Adam Mow suspended a one-year jail term; Kasimow did not speak at sentencing but had written an apology letter, according to the charges.

item.title: Possible new dinosaur species discovered at dig site near Arches National Park
item.description:
Fossils from the newly opened Ironstone Bonebed north of Arches National Park appear to belong to a previously unknown armored dinosaur species roughly 140 million years old, according to the Utah Geological Survey. State paleontologist Jim Kirkland, who leads the dig, hopes to name the species for assistant state paleontologist Don DeBlieux, his field partner of 25 years, who retires from the state at year's end. Because the site sits just above the Morrison Formation, it could help explain what followed the extinction event at the end of the Jurassic, and Kirkland expects "decades of work on this individual site".

item.title: Wisconsin infant is third measles-related death this week in US
item.description:
An infant has died in Wisconsin's largest measles outbreak in more than three decades, the state's first measles death in over 35 years and the third reported in the U.S. this week, after a child in New York's Lewis County and an unvaccinated resident of rural Pennsylvania. Wisconsin has logged 431 cases this year, compared with 36 in 2025, and with kindergarten MMR coverage at about 85%, well short of the roughly 95% needed, state epidemiologist Dr. Ryan Westergaard said the virus keeps "finding new hosts" among susceptible people. The state now recommends an early MMR dose for some at-risk infants ages 6 to 11 months, as the national count passes 4,800 cases, the most since 1991, ahead of an international review of U.S. elimination status next week.

item.title: Utahns vote to retain Supreme Court Justice Jill Pohlman, and other election updates
item.description:
More than 77% of Utah voters chose to retain Associate Chief Justice Jill Pohlman, the Supreme Court's highest-ranking member, despite calls from Rep. Burgess Owens and Utah Republican Party Chairman Rob Axson to vote her out amid GOP frustration over the court's rulings on abortion and redistricting. The AP called the 2nd Congressional District for Rep. Blake Moore on Thursday, leaving Rep. Mike Kennedy's lead in the 4th District as the only uncalled race, while Democrats stayed on pace to flip legislative seats and Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore trailed Shana Anderson by more than 4,000 votes. Forward Party Sen. Emily Buss trailed Republican Brooks Benson by fewer than 200 votes as counting continued, with Salt Lake County planning more result releases Thursday night and possibly through Saturday.

item.title: From Tonga to Utah's Capitol: Doug Fiefia celebrates historic Senate election
item.description:
Republican Rep. Doug Fiefia, who led Democrat A. Dane Anderson with about 55% of the unofficial vote in Senate District 18, is poised to become the first Tongan-American in the Utah Senate, a result he tied to the sacrifices of parents who immigrated from Tonga in the 1970s. Crediting more than 100 volunteers, his wife, Jocelyn, and a relative who served in the Utah House decades ago, Fiefia said he is "standing on the shoulders of people who came before me," and hopes Polynesian kids and others are inspired to serve. Having reached the race by ousting Sen. Dan McCay in the June primary, Fiefia, who has worked in the tech industry, named affordability, parental rights and growth as priorities, with online child safety a particular focus, arguing that "Parents shouldn't have to fight billion-dollar companies alone to protect their children".

item.title: Utah picks new mineral contractor for US Magnesium site, calls it a 'significant win'
item.description:
Gov. Spencer Cox called it a "significant win" that Texas-based Mariana Minerals will plan a phased restart of lithium and magnesium extraction at the former US Magnesium site on the Great Salt Lake, using low-water, non-evaporative methods in place of the site's large solar evaporation diversions. Utah bought the 4,500-acre property and its nearly 145,000 acre-feet of water rights for $30 million after the company's bankruptcy, and projects that royalties from the new operation could help pay for cleanup of what is also a Superfund site. Specific terms, including cleanup milestones, are still being finalized, and CEO Turner Caldwell said the aim is to transform the site into "a 21st-century operation that we can be proud of."

item.title: California Gov. Newsom says he will commute all death sentences in state to life without parole
item.description:
Gov. Gavin Newsom said he will commute the sentences of all 548 people on California's death row to life without parole, though the state Supreme Court must approve 382 of them, roughly 70%, because those inmates were convicted of a felony more than once. Newsom, who imposed a moratorium on executions in 2019 and is leaving office while weighing a presidential run, wrote that "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values," a stance the ACLU applauded. Prosecutors and some victims' relatives condemned the move, with San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow calling it a "sickening abuse of power", while Polly Klaas' sister Jess Nichol, whose views changed over time, said execution distracts from what survivors actually need.

item.title: Felony charges filed against Utah man following 3 1/2 hour standoff
item.description:
A 46-year-old Saratoga Springs man, David Glenn Logsdon, faces felony charges including assault on a police officer, aggravated assault and domestic violence in the presence of a child after a Halloween-night standoff that lasted 3 1/2 hours. Charging documents say Logsdon repeatedly pointed a handgun at his wife and at himself during an argument after both had been drinking while their 1-year-old granddaughter slept in the basement; after the wife fled and called 911, an officer team went in and brought the baby out safely. From an upstairs window he threw a monitor, bottles and books at officers and claimed he had "plenty of ammunition" until chemical munitions brought him out, and police found two handguns but no spent casing proving he had fired.

item.title: Trump meets at the White House with Putin envoy after he appeared with Melania Trump
item.description:
At a White House event honoring Melania Trump for brokering a six-day ceasefire in the occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, where nearly 800 people evacuated and aid was delivered, both Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Ukrainian officials thanked the first lady, who said she hoped it would be "the modest spark that grows into a lasting flame of peace". President Trump later said he met privately with Dmitriev but not with the Ukrainians, and predicted "a big agreement" that would involve more than Ukraine, possibly all of Europe. The AP notes the truce was the most significant since Russia's full-scale invasion and part of a broader foreign-policy role for the first lady, who has also helped reunite nearly three dozen children with their families.

item.title: Bingo, Care Bears, Pokémon cards, playground slide make it into the Toy Hall of Fame
item.description:
Care Bears got a boost from nearly 1 million social media followers, and Pokémon cards from anime and manga fans, on the way into the National Toy Hall of Fame, where they join bingo and the playground slide as this year's picks from 12 finalists. Curator Mirek Stolee noted that bingo, long associated with older players, has caught on with young adults in bars and nightclubs. Jeremy Saucier, vice president for collections, said people of all ages fondly remember "the simple, satisfying, and energizing experience of racing down a slide".

item.title: Massive tech sell-off wipes $2.5T from the stock market
item.description:
Fears that Democrats' midterm gains, notably Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's call for a temporary data center moratorium, could slow the AI buildout sent the Nasdaq down 5.52% into correction Thursday, erasing roughly $2.5 trillion in value, while the Dow gave back 1,833 points and all 11 S&P 500 sectors closed lower. Chip stocks led the rout, with Nvidia off 9.3% and a closely watched chipmaker index posting its worst day in about six and a half years, as the VIX jumped roughly 70% and the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.84%. Truist's Keith Lerner, who viewed the swings as more knee-jerk than predictive, said "the risk-reward is improving for longer-term investors," while Ed Yardeni welcomed a slowdown, saying the buildout "was too frenzied and speculative".

item.description:
Stocks tied to the AI data center buildout led a broad Wall Street sell-off Thursday that more than erased the previous day's rally, leaving the S&P 500 down 3.9% and on track for its worst drop since the April 2025 tariff shock, while the Nasdaq slid into correction territory, more than 10% below its October high. Nvidia fell 8.7% and AMD 15.5% amid worries about costly borrowing and the chance that Democratic midterm wins could lead governments to pause data center construction, though AppLovin jumped 28.5% on strong results. Easing Treasury yields hinted that investors were seeking safety, and in London the Bank of England raised rates for the first time in three years as Gov. item.title: Postal employee shot 2 coworkers at an Iowa post office before being captured, police say
item.description:
Police in Des Moines say a 39-year-old postal worker opened fire Thursday in a nonpublic second-floor area of the city's main post office, wounding two female coworkers, while a male employee was hurt in a fall as he tried to escape; all three were in stable condition. Officers arrived within three minutes and detained the unnamed suspect without resistance on a nearby bike path, where a 9 mm handgun was recovered, and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service is investigating with local, state and federal agencies. Earlier postal shootings, including a 1986 rampage in Edmond, Oklahoma, helped prompt a study released in 2000 that concluded "going postal" was a myth.

item.title: Utah leaders discuss homelessness solutions at statewide summit
item.description:
Gov. Spencer Cox gave the keynote at the Central Utah Homeless Summit in Salt Lake City, the last of three regional gatherings, saying homelessness "touches every community in the state". Organizers reported a 2% drop in homelessness in Utah and a 9.7% decline in unsheltered homelessness, and State Homeless Coordinator Tyler Clancy said the Legislature fully funded Cox's top budget priority with about $17 million in ongoing money and about $25 million in one-time infrastructure funding. Switchpoint CEO Carol Hollowell urged statewide cooperation, warning that without it "we're going to be in a bigger crisis in the next go around".

item.title: Russia and Ukraine trade airstrikes as reconstruction and security talks resume in Brussels
item.description:
Talks on Ukraine's postwar reconstruction, 2027 funding and Western-backed security guarantees ran for a second day at NATO headquarters in Brussels, with the World Bank and BlackRock attending alongside U.S., European and NATO officials, days before planned Russia-Ukraine-U.S. negotiations in Abu Dhabi. Overnight, Russia said it downed 496 Ukrainian drones, Kremlin-installed officials said a Ukrainian strike on a bus killed five people in occupied Luhansk, and rescuers kept searching for more than 30 people believed trapped after Monday's guided-bomb attack in Komyshuvakha, where Zelenskyy said 43 have been confirmed dead. The European Commission also sent Ukraine $4.9 billion from a $101 billion EU loan, and Zelenskyy told German broadcaster ZDF he hoped the Democrats' midterm win would help renew U.S.-European ties while adding that "I am also grateful to the Republicans".

item.title: California resident is latest to be charged in Utah tap-to-pay scam
item.description:
Prosecutors charged Liu Huan, 36, of Irvine, California, in 4th District Court with money laundering, theft by deception and other felonies, alleging tap-to-pay purchases since Oct. 1 in St. George, Orem, Sandy, Midvale, Salt Lake City and Draper. In these scams, phones loaded with stolen card numbers are tapped on self-checkout devices to buy gift cards or electronics, with gift card numbers sent to a handler who quickly moves the funds, and investigators believe a "criminal enterprise" of Chinese nationals headquartered in China, with U.S. bases in California and New York, is sending people to Utah. Police found dozens of gift cards and receipts plus boxed electronics in Huan's vehicle, and the charges say Huan admitted buying two gift cards for $980 and sending screenshots to a person in China for a promised $100.

item.title: Unemployment claims drop to 189,000, the fewest since mid-July
item.description:
Weekly claims have stayed at or below 200,000 for eight weeks running, and the latest Labor Department count of 189,000 initial jobless claims is the lowest since mid-July, a sign that layoffs remain rare. Hiring is a weaker story: employers have added about 68,000 jobs a month this year and only 29,000 last month, though that still beats 2025's average of 9,700. Forecasters surveyed by FactSet expect Friday's October report to show 65,000 new jobs, with unemployment holding at 4.2%.

item.title: 2 unaffiliated candidates poised to win seats in Utah Legislature
item.description:
Utah could see its first independent general-election winners in modern history, as unaffiliated candidates Patrick Belmont and Sergio Sotelo lead races for Republican-held House seats: Belmont is ahead of Rep. Jason Thompson by more than 1,700 votes in Cache County, and Sotelo leads by nearly 1,100 in the open seat vacated by Rep. Cheryl Acton, where Republican Chris McConnehey has conceded. Belmont, a Utah State University professor who lost a 2024 bid, argued that "we have got to get away from party politics" and drop labels, while Sotelo, a longtime IBEW electrician, said his backers span parties and "vote with our pockets." Party records are spotty, but BYU's Adam Brown said no Utah legislator has lacked a party affiliation since at least 1934, and the Legislature's lone third-party member, appointed Forward Party Sen. Emily Buss, narrowly trails in her own race.

item.title: Wendy's rejects buyout bid and girds itself for a hostile takeover campaign
item.description:
Wendy's board adopted a one-year "poison pill" plan, triggered when anyone holds 15% or more of its shares, after independent directors unanimously turned down a $1.4 billion offer from Nelson Peltz's investor group, which already holds 16.3% of the stock, saying the bid "substantially undervalues" the company. CEO Bob Wright, the chain's fourth chief executive since 2024, argued that his Dave's Way turnaround, from thicker bacon and creamier Frosties to a slimmer menu, is already working, and third-quarter revenue of $547 million beat analysts' forecast even as same-store sales fell 5.2%. Peltz, who chaired the Wendy's board for 17 years until 2024, had pitched his offer as the best path for shareholders amid high beef prices, aging stores and pressured consumers.

item.title: State argues it alone should investigate leftover evidence after overturned 1985 murder conviction
item.description:
Utah County prosecutors told the court this week that they intend to run forensic genealogy testing themselves on what remains of the evidence in the 1985 killing of Eva Olesen, opposing a request from Doug Carter's attorneys to do their own testing after DNA results found none of Carter's DNA and the knife carried only the victim's profile and an unknown man's. Prosecutor Christopher Ballard wrote that the investigation is ongoing and that the samples must be preserved for any future defendant, while the state still insists Carter is the killer, pointing to a confession the defense says was coerced and whose recording was destroyed. Defense attorney Neal Hamilton questioned why prosecutors waited until he sought a court order, saying "Their case has fallen apart" and that the state "stole 41 years of Doug's life" on death row.

item.title: The rivalry forecast: KSL Sports experts give their game-day predictions
item.description:
Ahead of Saturday's 10 a.m. BYU-Utah kickoff in Salt Lake City, KSL Sports' Sam Farnsworth predicted BYU will turn Utah's 23-year streak of interceptions for touchdowns around by returning one itself in the second half, and said Byrd Ficklin could lead the Utes in rushing and even throw a touchdown pass. Jeremiah Jensen framed the game around quarterbacks, saying BYU's Bear Bachmeier must repeat his Notre Dame form while Utah's Devon Dampier gets a chance to make up for last year, and suggested the morning start could take some edge off a crowd that is loud and chaotic at night. The two agreed only that something unexpected is coming, or as Jensen put it, "Every year there is gonna be a crazy play."

item.title: El Niño has brought flooding. It's also slowly lifting Utah out of drought
item.description:
Weeks of El Niño-driven rain have shrunk Utah's drought footprint from over 90% of the state to about two-thirds in one week, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor, with parts of the Uintas and southeast Utah out of any drought category for the first time since June 2025, and the share in severe or extreme drought falling to about 36%. Mountain soil moisture has climbed to nearly 78% saturation, above the typical spring peak, which Utah Snow Survey director Jordan Clayton described as "uncharted territory," and Gunlock Reservoir went from 37% full to over 100% while Lake Powell rose 17 feet in a month. Still, the statewide reservoir system sits at just 50% of capacity after this year's record-low snowpack, and Clayton said it is too early to know how the soggy fall will shape conditions over the coming months.

item.title: Bob the poet, meet Bob the priest: Pope Leo XIV receives Bob Dylan at the Vatican
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV, the Chicago-born pontiff born Robert Prevost, received Bob Dylan in a private audience at the Vatican's apostolic palace on Wednesday, a meeting the Vatican newspaper confirmed using Dylan's birth name, Robert Allen Zimmerman. Leo has already quoted an unpublished 1963 Dylan anti-nuclear protest song in the preface to a collection of his addresses, in keeping with the church's opposition to nuclear weapons that he has emphasized, and Dylan once performed for Pope John Paul II at a 1997 church event in Bologna. The Rev. Antonio Spadaro, the Vatican official who brokered the visit after arranging Leo's earlier meeting with Patti Smith, wrote that the encounter had "a real sense of history about it".

item.title: Utah Food Bank faces growing challenges as holiday demand rises
item.description:
As holiday demand rises, Utah Food Bank president and CEO Ginette Bott says monetary donations give the organization the most flexibility as costs climb, especially fuel for its fleet of about 70 delivery vehicles. Bott said flooding has created obstacles for the food bank's southern Utah pantries, and some communities are losing service from local pantries, adding strain to its distribution network. The food bank is also seeking nutritious food donations, and Bott urged shoppers to buy extra groceries because "Everything your family loves, another family will enjoy".

item.title: Cache Valley Humanitarian Center turns volunteer hours into millions of dollars in aid
item.description:
The Cache Valley Humanitarian Center, which opened in July 2021 with a $2,000 grant from two Logan Rotary Clubs, has produced more than $2 million worth of newborn kits, hygiene kits, sleeping mats, quilts and other items for people in need, according to co-founder and executive director Dwight Whittaker. Whittaker counts about 45,000 volunteer hours so far, and the center works with about 30 nonprofits and three school districts in an area stretching from Wellsville to Preston, Idaho. Volunteer Cloteel Liechty, 97, said the work "makes my day," and the center welcomes more individual volunteers and groups, especially youth groups.

item.title: 'That was not discipline': Man accused of attempting to drown daughter sentenced
item.description:
Andres Blas Hernandez, 46, who was accused of holding his daughter under the San Pitch River and pleaded guilty to two counts of child endangerment and a drug misdemeanor, had his prison terms suspended and was ordered to serve 270 days in jail and three years of probation with anger management, substance abuse and mental health requirements. His daughter told the court she wanted prison because "I could have died that day and he did not care," while Hernandez apologized and insisted he "intended to get the phone wet, and that was it." Sixth District Judge Robert Van Dyke said the conduct had built over time rather than being a single incident, pointing to Hernandez's earlier prison time and failed probation.

item.title: Cornell rape investigation will be led by a former prosecutor in the Sean 'Diddy' Combs case
item.description:
New York Attorney General Letitia James named Jacqueline Kelly, a Cornell alumna and former Manhattan federal prosecutor who oversaw sex crimes cases against Sean Combs and Peter Nygård, to lead the reopened investigation into a former student's allegation that several men raped her at a fraternity party in October 2024. Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor on Oct. 1 after losing faith in Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who declined to bring charges in 2024, and two men named in the student's lawsuit are now seeking James' removal over a social media post supporting the accuser that she made before her appointment. Kelly, who will remain at Boies Schiller Flexner during the probe, said "All New Yorkers deserve a fair and thorough inquiry into the facts of this case".

item.title: What's next in the investigation of the Learjet crash in Florida that killed 9?
item.description:
The NTSB investigation into the Bahamas-bound Learjet that crashed in Florida after encountering a thunderstorm, killing all nine aboard, will likely take more than a year, though a preliminary report without analysis of the cause is expected about 30 days after the crash. Pieces of the tail's elevator found more than a mile from the main crater confirm the jet began breaking apart before impact, and NTSB member Tom Chapman said the cockpit voice recorder would be "very important data" but that not finding it wouldn't doom the probe. Weather will be an early focus, with retired airline pilot John Cox saying "I don't understand why they came down" from 41,000 feet near the storms, while investigators also review maintenance records and interview the operator, Upper Jets, and air traffic controllers.

item.title: Romney blames GOP midterm losses on 'bad policy, bad character'
item.description:
Former Sen. Mitt Romney wrote on social media that Republicans' midterm losses came down to "Bad policy, bad character", listing grievances from erratic tariffs and the Iran war to blanket pardons, ICE brutality and hiding Epstein, and said he hoped for a course correction. Other Republicans offered their own explanations: Vice President JD Vance said the Iran war was "the reason we lost," while Utah Sen. John Curtis called the election a wake-up call for a party he suggested had abandoned core conservative principles. Democrats, who flipped both chambers with some races still pending, credited affordability and dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump.

item.title: Salt Lake County continues processing more than 100,000 ballots as key races remain unsettled
item.description:
Salt Lake County is still verifying more than 100,000 mail ballots dropped off on Election Day, a process Clerk Lannie Chapman said now takes roughly 12 seconds per ballot instead of two to three because a new state law adds a check of the last four digits of a voter's Social Security number or Utah ID to signature matching. Early returns suggest Democrats could gain control of the County Council and voters appear to be backing a $128 million parks and recreation bond, though Chapman cautioned "we still have a lot of ballots to count." Officials hope to release more totals Thursday evening and Friday, provisional ballots will be added next week, and certification will follow the two-week canvass period in which voters can cure ballot problems.

item.title: Florida authorities say 2 dead at Tampa office complex, including gunman shot by security guard
item.description:
A gunman drove a car into a courtyard where people were eating lunch on Citibank's Tampa business campus Wednesday and killed a woman with a rifle before a security guard confronted him in a cafeteria and fatally shot him, according to the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office, which gave no motive and did not say whether the two knew each other. Chief Deputy Frank Losat said about 3,200 people were working on the campus, four others were hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries and more than 360 deputies spent 2 1/2 hours clearing buildings, and he offered "kudos to that security guard" for preventing potential further violence. A nearby Sheraton sheltered an estimated 300 Citibank workers, and a Citibank vice president recalled an "incredible clatter" he later realized was gunfire.

item.title: Ogden man sentenced to 15 years to life imprisonment in killing of his mother
item.description:
Alec Conrad Martinez, 27, was sentenced Monday in 2nd District Court to 15 years to life in prison for murdering his mother, Jennifer Martinez, in Ogden in 2025, after pleading guilty in July while citing a mental condition. Under the plea deal, the Weber County Attorney's Office dismissed counts of attempting to disarm an officer of a taser and use of a dangerous weapon by a restricted person. According to the account of the June 19 emergency calls, the mother screamed "He has a knife!" before the line went silent, and Martinez then called dispatchers to say he thought he had killed her.

item.title: The Southern Taurid meteor shower will bring rare fireballs tonight
item.description:
The Southern Taurid meteor shower produces only about five meteors an hour but is known for bright fireballs from marble- to boulder-sized debris shed by comet 2P/Encke, with viewing expected to be best around midnight Thursday and the peak estimated around 3 p.m. ET on Nov. 5, according to EarthSky. NASA's Bill Cooke said "when you see one, you'll remember it" and advised finding a dark spot and giving eyes at least half an hour to adjust without a phone, while astronomer Bethany Cobb Kung suggests locating Orion's belt and looking to the right toward Taurus. Cooke said Earth is predicted to pass through a denser swarm of Taurid debris in 2032, describing the present as "a lull before the thunderstorms occur."
