item.title: Southern Utah couple accused of abusing young daughter
item.description:
Trevor Dean Noffsinger, 22, and Mariah Faith Calapp, 21, of Cedar City were booked into the Iron County Jail on Tuesday for investigation of aggravated child abuse after an investigation that began in February, when doctors found their 4-month-old daughter had clavicle and rib fractures in different stages of healing along with grip-pattern bruising that medical staff deemed non-accidental. According to a police affidavit, Calapp admitted lying to a nurse about the cause, while Noffsinger told police "I believe it might have been me" but said he didn't hurt the baby on purpose and blamed palm bruising on not knowing his own strength. Police also noted Noffsinger's prior child abuse conviction and the 2024 death of the couple's infant son, ruled a sudden unexplained infant death, whom Calapp said had the same palm bruising.

item.title: 'It wasn't just a home': Flooding displaces generations of a family near Bluff
item.description:
Kayla Atcitty's grandmothers, cousins and other relatives were displaced when San Juan River flooding near Bluff reached homes in a family community whose roots trace back to her great-great-grandfather, with water rising from shin- to thigh-deep within about an hour as they fled with documents, medications and animals. One grandmother and four cousins are now in Atcitty's basement, bringing her household to 10, while another grandmother is in an RV park cabin near Blanding, and the family doesn't know whether the homes will be livable given worries about water under the structures and mold. Atcitty, whose own parents lost their home there in a 2003 flood, said "It wasn't just a home that they lost," and has started a GoFundMe for the family.

item.title: A 24-year-old running the NYC marathon collapsed 2 miles from the finish line and died
item.description:
Rachel Apa, 24, of Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, collapsed a couple of miles short of the finish in her first New York City Marathon on Sunday and died at a hospital; the medical examiner is still investigating, though her father told the New York Times the cause was rhabdomyolysis, a rare condition in which skeletal muscle breaks down and poisons the body. Mount Sinai nephrologist Doug Farrell, who documented 24 rhabdo cases at the unusually hot 2022 race, said heat speeds muscle breakdown, though Sunday's temperatures hovered in the mid-60s. Emory sports cardiologist Jonathan Kim said deaths from rhabdo "would be really, really rare", noting that heart attack is the most common cause of cardiac arrest in marathons and that runners' chance of dying from sudden cardiac arrest fell by half from 2010 to 2023.

item.title: JetBlue raises baggage fees a second time as jet fuel prices stay elevated
item.description:
JetBlue has raised checked bag fees for the second time this year, so most economy passengers on tickets bought on or after Nov. 3 will pay at least $50 each way for a first bag, up from $39, and as much as $70 when paying within 24 hours of a peak-period departure. The airline's March increase helped set off bag-fee hikes at Delta, United, American and Southwest, and JetBlue said in the spring that the increases help offset higher operating costs while keeping base fares competitive. Jet fuel prices have stayed elevated because the unresolved Iran war has largely restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, and JetBlue expects its average fuel price to reach $4.64 a gallon in the final three months of the year, up 85% from a year earlier.

item.title: These Salt Lake City blocks inspired Smith Entertainment Group's downtown plan
item.description:
New design guidelines from Smith Entertainment Group for its planned downtown district draw on Salt Lake City areas such as Main Street, Regent Street, the 2nd & 2nd District and 9th & 9th, which executive Mike Maughan said the company wants to learn from rather than recreate, aiming for something "uniquely Salt Lake" instead of the mountain and red rock motifs common in Utah pitches. City leaders were surprised that building heights may top out near half the zone's 600-foot maximum, Council Chairman Alejandro Puy said, but they're encouraged by plans to break up the Salt Palace and raise 200 West, and they believe a proposed 6,000-seat music venue was placed to limit impacts on Japantown, where community members raised concerns. An updated development agreement could be drafted by year's end, with a Planning Commission presentation tentatively set for Dec. 9 and a partial demolition of the convention center slated to begin in February or March.

According to the charges, he said that if the children called police he would "make sure he took officers with him," and police say he later brandished a gun at officers during an armed standoff in Syracuse and was shot. Police asked that Dicus be held until trial as a "lethal threat", and Syracuse police said more charges may follow once the officer-involved shooting investigation concludes.

item.title: Utah House Republicans may lose supermajority for first time in decades
item.description:
Utah Republicans appear on track to lose their two-thirds supermajority in the state House for the first time this century, with 15 sitting GOP lawmakers trailing their challengers on Wednesday and the caucus possibly shrinking from 61 seats to as few as 44, which would leave it unable to override vetoes or propose constitutional amendments without Democratic votes; Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore also trailed Democrat Shana Anderson by more than 4,000 votes. Incumbents blamed a national wave compounded by their own missteps, with Rep. Matt MacPherson calling the decision to put Amendment B on the ballot a likely strategic error, though Rep. Norm Thurston, trailing by nearly 600 votes, noted that only about half of Utah County's ballots had been counted. Taylor Morgan of Morgan May Public Affairs described "the blue bludgeoning" reaching Utah, while BYU political scientist Adam Brown attributed the losses chiefly to dissatisfaction with the Trump administration, saying down-ballot races are driven by "what's happening at the top".

item.title: NASA space telescope plunges to Earth after 2 decades studying cosmic explosions
item.description:
NASA's Swift Observatory reentered the atmosphere near Indonesia on Wednesday, ending a study of gamma ray bursts and exploding stars that was planned for two years but lasted 22, after solar activity dragged down its orbit and a robotic orbit-boost attempt by Katalyst Space failed when that craft came down in September. NASA anticipated that some denser pieces of the 1 1/2-ton spacecraft would survive reentry. The agency is now asking private companies how they might boost, upgrade or safely deorbit the Hubble Space Telescope, which recent analyses expect to come down by the mid-2030s, and Administrator Jared Isaacman said the telescope "still has important science ahead of it".

Come and See's Stacey Baxter said "Now the work is to take it to the world," noting that the series app drew 2.2 million international users in October, compared with 1.6 million in the United States. Season 6 premieres Nov. 15 on Prime Video, and the first season already holds a Guinness World Records title as the most-translated television season, in 125 languages.

item.description:
Democrats won unusually wide majorities in both chambers, with Senate Democrats holding at least 54 seats after long-shot pickups in South Carolina, Texas and Kansas, and they plan a 100-day agenda on gas, grocery and health care costs alongside broad oversight of the Trump administration, with impeachment an option. Trump signaled he could work with Democrats while threatening vetoes and acknowledged the Iran war affected the vote, and Vice President JD Vance pointedly wrote that "The reason we lost is the war". Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and council member Nithya Raman, a challenger backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, were in a tight race in early returns Wednesday, with Raman holding a slim advantage and an estimated one-third of ballots still uncounted. Bass, backed by Gavin Newsom, Kamala Harris and Nancy Pelosi, has called Raman "not ready for primetime" and her views on policing and homelessness extreme, while Raman has pledged to cut the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least 50% by 2028. The incumbent still faces fallout from the 2025 Palisades Fire, and a Raman win would place her alongside New York's Zohran Mamdani among democratic socialists leading city governments.

The other two races were still being counted: in Davis County, unaffiliated former commissioner Bret Millburn narrowly led Republican Susan Lee 50.7% to 49.3%, though Millburn noted as many as 30,000 ballots remain uncounted, and in Weber County, Republican Duane Kearsley led Democrat Alvin Thurgood 49.2% to 45.2%. item.title: CVS to split into two companies, in major breakup of its $117B healthcare empire
item.description:
CVS Health will separate into two companies in a tax-free transaction expected to close in early 2028, reversing a strategy that began with its 2007 Caremark merger and continued with its $69 billion purchase of Aetna in 2018. CEO David Joyner described the move as "taking what I believe is one great company and making it two," and the split isn't expected to change how people shop at CVS or what patients pay for prescriptions. It cuts against an industry trend toward integrated conglomerates that consumer advocates and lawmakers blame for higher costs, and CVS shares fell 10% in early trading even as the company reported stronger third-quarter results and raised its guidance.

item.title: First lady Abby Cox wrote a children's book
item.description:
Utah first lady Abby Cox read her new children's book, Jennie Makes Room, to students in the Governor's Mansion ballroom, telling the story of philanthropist Jennie Judge Kearns, whose giving helped fund an orphanage that became Kearns-Saint Ann Catholic School, helped finance the Cathedral of the Madeleine and supplied the mansion now used as the governor's residence. Cox said she "realized how much my work intersected with the things that she was passionate about", and said proceeds will go to the Mansion Foundation to preserve the home, whose details are hidden throughout Matt Loveridge's illustrations. The school's principal, a great-great-granddaughter of Kearns, noted that the students were walking through the home of the family whose generosity helped make their school possible.

item.title: Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race, will be first Muslim senator
item.description:
Progressive Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers for Michigan's open Senate seat and will become the nation's first Muslim senator, after a grassroots campaign built on Medicare for All and sharp criticism of Israel that survived nearly $30 million in AIPAC spending against him in the primary. Rogers struggled to stay aligned with Trump amid high fuel prices and an unpopular war with Iran, while Republicans sought to link El-Sayed to terrorist organizations without evidence. "They might have been pointing to my name and my faith, but we all know my name and my faith are not why you can't afford your gas," El-Sayed said in his victory speech, a result that gives progressives an argument heading into 2028 that their agenda can win in battleground states.

item.title: 2 rescued from southern Utah reservoir that received a rare fall surge
item.description:
Washington County search and rescue crews and local firefighters pulled two people from the roof of their Toyota Tacoma on Monday after it became stuck crossing the river near the Gunlock Reservoir waterfalls and water began entering the cab. The reservoir surged from 37% capacity last month to 109% as of Tuesday after several nearby mountain locations received more than 8 inches of precipitation in October, a sharp contrast with its typical fall rise of about one percentage point. With record-high soil moisture and long-range forecasts showing no sign of a break in the stormy pattern, sheriff's officials warned that "Even familiar crossings can quickly become dangerous" and urged people never to drive through swift-moving water.

item.title: Power customers in 16 Utah communities face fee hike for renewable energy program
item.description:
About 250,000 Rocky Mountain Power customers in 16 communities, including Salt Lake City, Park City, Moab and Ogden, will be automatically enrolled Jan. 1 in the Community Clean Energy Program, which adds $4 a month to residential bills and a usage-based fee for businesses to fund wind, solar and other renewable resources under HB411, a 2019 law. Customers can avoid the fee by opting out by Dec. 31 and can leave without a termination fee through May 1, after which a one-time $30 charge applies, a charge Salt Lake City's Glade Sowards said "isn't punitive" but meant to gauge interest. Kamas-area resident Dee Warner, surprised by the notification letter, opted out and accused those behind the program of "going behind our backs".

item.description:
Recent flooding sent water and mud through the Bluff Historic Fort in San Juan County, forcing volunteers to empty 13 cabins and wash, dry and treat the chairs, beds and other furniture before returning them. Co-director Connie Hunt said people from every state have called to ask whether the fort, which tells the story of pioneers who reached Bluff in 1880 and remains open, was saved, and she joked that unlike the settlers she has "a pressure washer" and a crew of 100.

item.title: Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff wins reelection, defeating Rep. Mike Collins to hold a key Democratic seat
item.description:
Sen. Jon Ossoff, 39, won a second term Tuesday by defeating Trump-endorsed Republican Rep. Mike Collins, holding what had been a top GOP target as the only Senate Democrat seeking reelection in a state Trump carried in 2024. Ossoff ran as an aggressive Trump critic, raised more than $100 million amid 2028 speculation, and repeatedly branded Collins a "bigot" over past posts and associates' white nationalist ties, while Collins struggled with fundraising and an unresolved House ethics investigation. The AP calls the win a "notably bitter confirmation" of Trump's slide toward lame-duck status in the state where he anchored his false claims about the 2020 election.

item.title: Jury begins deliberating at Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault trial
item.description:
Jurors at London's Southwark Crown Court began deliberating Tuesday in Russell Brand's trial after three weeks of evidence, with Judge Joel Bennathan telling them their verdict must be unanimous. Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault involving six women between 1999 and 2009, and he testified that his encounters were consensual. His lawyer, Ian Winter, argued the women went to police only after a 2023 documentary that left the "well of justice" tainted, and told jurors, "It is not criminal to treat women unkindly before, during or after sex."

item.title: 'Drop what you have and just come talk to us,' police order before fatal shooting
item.description:
West Valley City police released body camera video Tuesday showing an officer spending about three minutes urging Sebastian Enrique Cerda-Monti, 40, to drop what he held and leave a storage shed outside a TownePlace Suites hotel on Oct. 25, at one point using pepper spray, before Cerda-Monti charged him waving two silver objects 2 to 3 feet long. The officer fired 10 to 12 shots and Cerda-Monti died at the scene despite immediate aid, after a hotel employee's 911 call reported he had threatened to shoot workers trying to enter. West Jordan police will investigate for the Salt Lake County District Attorney's Office, and court records show Cerda-Monti had been sentenced to time served a week earlier for mail theft and failing to stop for police.

item.title: It's Election Day: Here's why 12 election monitors are in Utah
item.description:
Twelve of the Justice Department's 1,000 federal election monitors were assigned to Utah, all in Salt Lake County, where Clerk Lannie Chapman said she has "No concerns" and noted the monitors, mostly Utah residents, are expected to check compliance with Spanish-language materials and disability access laws. Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson said they will work in pairs at six or seven sites under the standard observer rules, such as staying six feet from booths, and that while the scale is unusual, federal monitors visiting states is normal. The Utah League of Women Voters and ACLU of Utah, which have trained about 150 poll watchers who will also watch the monitors, warned the lack of specifics could intimidate voters, with Helen Moser calling the effort "kind of capricious."

item.title: Salt Lake City plan for a year-round Downtown Farmers Market building fizzles
item.description:
The Salt Lake City Downtown Alliance has dropped its plan for a permanent, year-round Downtown Farmers Market building at Pioneer Park, an estimated $20 million to $25 million project endorsed by Mayor Erin Mendenhall, after a year and a half of talks failed to settle ownership and financing. City real estate adviser Blake Thomas said "it came down to the funding" because the city had no budget allocation for the building, though it would revisit the idea if that changed. The alliance will instead pursue a permanent winter market home, returning to the old Leonardo Museum building for a market starting Nov. 14, the day after the renovated park reopens.

item.title: Polls begin to close in midterm elections as voters pass judgment on Trump's second term
item.description:
Polls began closing Tuesday in midterm elections framed as a referendum on President Donald Trump's second term, with Republicans bracing to lose the House and fighting to hold the Senate, where Democrats need a net gain of four seats, after more than 59 million early ballots surpassed 2022's early turnout. The AP Voter Poll found about three-quarters of voters angry or dissatisfied with the country's direction and about 8 in 10 reporting inflation-related hardship, even as Trump told Fox News that "inflation is solved" despite 3.6% annual price growth in September. Key contests include Texas, where Trump-backed Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico, plus North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio and Alaska, and a Democratic chamber could open investigations into figures such as Pete Hegseth and Elon Musk.

item.description:
Last-minute voters filled some Salt Lake County ballot drop boxes to capacity by mid-morning on Election Day, and County Clerk Lannie Chapman said many people waited until the final 24 hours, so collection teams kept emptying boxes throughout the day. Voter Nicole Masco said the older she gets, the more important it is to have a say, calling it "a no-brainer" to do her civic duty. Collected ballots go through signature and registration checks before counting, and officials urged anyone still holding a ballot to use an official drop box before polls closed at 8 p.m.

item.title: Death toll hits 31 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, with dozens still missing
item.description:
Russian strikes with bunker-busting bombs on a former school and a shelter where people were lining up for humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, killed at least 31 people, including four police officers and two rescue workers, with more than 45 still missing. Acting regional head Mykhailo Semikin called it "one of the worst tragedies" for civilians in the region since the full-scale war began, and the attack came after a six-day ceasefire in Oleshky expired, which Zelenskyy said Ukraine had offered to extend. An overnight barrage of 289 drones and 76 missiles also hit power plants and hospitals across nine regions ahead of U.S.-mediated peace talks set for Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi, where Zelenskyy wants a halt to strikes on energy infrastructure.

item.title: Election Day unfolds with relatively few problems including weather, machine issues
item.description:
Relatively few voting problems had been reported by 4:30 p.m. MST Tuesday, with the biggest disruptions caused by flooding in Florida and the Southwest, where Navajo Nation officials moved polling sites and Utah's San Juan County let voters cast ballots electronically. In New York's Westchester County, a program update left scanners rejecting paper ballots, which went into emergency bags for later counting, and Broward County, Florida, started 20 minutes late after a new safety feature malfunctioned. Despite the Justice Department's largest-ever poll-monitoring effort and an ICE post warning noncitizen voters "There will be no escape," none of the federal steps Democrats most feared had happened, and David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation and Research called the smooth day "remarkable."

Weber County Clerk/Auditor Ricky Hatch, whose team set up 100 voting booths at the county fairgrounds on election eve, said this year has been a struggle of "seeing them as a threat" rather than a partner, referring to the federal government, which had sought voters' Social Security and driver's license numbers in a Justice Department suit a judge dismissed 10 days ago. Turnout was 38% Monday morning, on par for a midterm, and Hatch expects 60% to 65%, adding, "We love boring elections." Ballots must arrive by 8 p.m., and those dropped off late on Election Day may not be counted until Wednesday.

A weekend storm dropped 17 inches at Snowbird and let several resorts begin making snow, with Solitude scheduled to open Nov. 20 and Alta pausing uphill travel for snowmaking. Brighton's Jared Winkler said crews must take advantage of cold temperatures because it "can warm up (in) late November," and he hopes for at least an average winter after a rough last season. Super El Niño projections vary, but an Alta spokesperson said the odds favor more snow than last year.

item.title: Flights across Europe face disruption after false bomb threats
item.description:
Hoax bomb threats Tuesday targeted LOT, SAS and Ryanair flights across Europe, prompting diversions, searches and an Italian Air Force Eurofighter escort for a Dublin-to-Rome plane, a day after a Wizz Air flight from Luton was diverted to Budapest; no explosives were found and no one was hurt. Matthew Borie of Osprey Flight Solutions said the focus on Europe means "there could be a Russian angle," though Iranian hybrid warfare is also active there, and his advice to travelers was "Don't be alarmed." Greek authorities separately searched and evacuated the Israeli-run cruise ship Crown Iris at Syros as a precaution after a bomb threat.

item.title: Job postings jumped sharply in September, potentially good sign for those seeking employment
item.description:
Job openings rose to 7.5 million in September from a revised 7.19 million, the most since May, while gross hiring increased, layoffs fell to 1.64 million, the fewest since March 2025, and quits reached an 18-month high, so openings now exceed the number of unemployed. Navy Federal Credit Union economist Heather Long called the data "an encouraging sign" despite high fuel prices and inflation, but ZipRecruiter's Nicole Bachaud warned that inflation and higher interest rates will likely remain "a downward pressure on hiring." Friday's October jobs report is forecast to show 65,000 jobs added, a modest figure that the AP notes can still keep unemployment low as baby boomers retire and immigration falls.

A 40-year-old Hillcrest High School health sciences teacher who has not been charged resigned Monday, and Unified police forwarded his case to the Salt Lake County District Attorney's Office after saying he pointed his concealed handgun at his classroom door during a Sept. 30 lockdown drill as administrators and officers checked doors. A search warrant affidavit says 27 students were inside as he knelt behind a table aiming through the door's window, and that he told police he didn't know about the drill but couldn't describe any threat that justified his actions. Canyons School District spokesman Jeff Haney said drills are announced in advance and teachers with valid permits may carry guns, and that the teacher, with the district since 2018, was placed on paid leave the day of the drill.

Giamanco climbed in through a window and shot the attacker, Griffin J. Students must compete in two different sports or event categories through the Utah High School Athletic Association, the Summer Games or both, and qualifying events this month include Special Olympics Utah Unified Flag Football and the 1A-3A Eight-Player Football Championships. Jordan Virtual Learning Academy, made up of Rocky Peak Virtual Elementary, Kesley Peak Virtual Middle School and Kings Peak High School, pairs online instruction from certified teachers with in-person sessions two to three times a week and serves about 4,500 K-12 students. Any student with a Utah address can enroll, and Principal David Hullinger said families ranging from traveling athletes to students with anxieties want virtual school but "don't like their student only in front of a computer all day." item.title: Utah's soil moisture levels jump to 'uncharted territory.' Here's why that matters
item.description:
After what is expected to be one of Utah's wettest Octobers on record, statewide mountain soil moisture reached nearly 78% saturation, about four points above the usual spring-runoff peak, a reading Utah Snow Survey director Jordan Clayton called "uncharted territory." Wet fall soils typically make spring snowmelt more efficient, and reservoirs have already risen from 46% to 49%, but the saturation has also fueled flash flooding and landslides, and Clayton cautioned that "The snow has to come." Last year shows the risk: strong fall soil moisture was followed by Utah's worst snowpack on record.

The Janet L. Herrick Dementia-Friendly Choir in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, brings together more than 30 people living with dementia, caregivers and others touched by the disease, and director Carra-lyn Conger said music helps people with memory loss stay active by triggering different parts of the brain. Julie Messner, who has never missed a rehearsal and whose mother and husband both had dementia before dying in 2019, urged people to love such family members "like they were still ones you fell in love with." item.title: Stroke survivor grateful for therapy that helped him with new passion of woodworking
item.description:
David Wilson, 64, a retired principal who skied and golfed avidly before a January 2024 stroke, regained use of his left hand through an emerging therapy that combines transcranial electrical and magnetic stimulation with intense hand exercises, now under study at the University of Utah. Dr. Amit Sethi said the treatment, given three times a week for six weeks, helps intact brain areas take over for damaged ones, and his five-year study is still seeking participants. Wilson has since found a new passion making wooden bowls, including a walnut chopping board for Sethi, and said "The stroke closed doors, yet at the same time, it opened other doors."

item.title: Trump administration has slow-walked 380K potential immigrant voters
item.description:
USCIS approved about 55,000 citizenship requests from April to June, down from more than 230,000 a year earlier, and Stateline estimates almost 380,000 more immigrants, nearly all adults, could have become citizens and potential midterm voters had the earlier pace held. USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler attributed the slowdown to tougher vetting, including social media screening and stricter English and civics requirements, writing that "Naturalization is a privilege, not a right," while the National Partnership for New Americans accused the administration of deliberately delaying people's civil and voting rights. Matthew Morrison Bates, 42, of Lehi, pleaded guilty Monday in federal court to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering in a Ponzi scheme that prosecutors say took more than $60 million from "hundreds of investors" between May 2020 and June 2025. item.description:

Fillmore said a 2024 Utah Supreme Court ruling leaves lawmakers treating citizen initiatives as "untouchable," and California-focused policy analysts said a higher bar would guard Utah against special interests seeking tax increases. item.title: Supermarket freezers in several European countries hit by apparent cyberattacks
item.description:
Fridges and freezers in supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland and Estonia malfunctioned Monday in apparent cyberattacks, following a case last month in which attackers remotely seized refrigeration systems in hundreds of French stores. A Swedish ICA Kvantum store said its units were hacked and set to 50 degrees Celsius, Delhaize reported an "IT incident" at several dozen stores, Carrefour said 15 of its more than 700 Belgian stores were hit, and Ireland's Musgrave Group pulled chilled and frozen goods at 13 SuperValu stores. item.description:
Argentine President Javier Milei is courting AI data centers with a no-regulation pitch, telling the U.S. Chamber of Commerce "We are not going to regulate artificial intelligence," and proposing to cut the corporate tax rate to 15% from 25% for projects of at least $1 billion, while Patagonia offers cold weather, wind, open land and Vaca Muerta shale gas. Polish firm Green Capital, which has yet to secure a customer, plans a $3 billion Patagonian campus on land leased from sheep ranchers that at peak would use about 2.7 times Buenos Aires' 2025 electricity, according to an AP calculation. Critics note the incentives require no local computing capacity or disclosure of energy and water use, a Córdoba computer science professor warned Argentina could become "a laboratory," and a small group of Trelew residents has rallied against data centers.

item.title: Which party cares about passing down their politics? New survey finds answer
item.description:
The American Family Survey of 2,000 Americans, by the Deseret News, the Wheatley Institute and BYU's Center for the Study of Elections and Democracy, found most Americans don't consider passing their political beliefs to their children important, but Republicans are twice as likely as Democrats to say it is. Co-author Jeremy Pope said researchers "don't know why that difference exists" and speculated that Democrats may focus on passing down values rather than beliefs, while a 2023 Pew study found teens of Democratic parents matched their parents' party more often (89% vs. 81%). University of Utah student organizer Samantha Reagan, raised by Democrats and now a self-described socialist, said she kept her parents' moral values, such as caring for the poor, more than their politics.

The William A. Burnard Warming Center, housed in Logan's St. John's Episcopal Church, opened its fifth season Nov. 2 and will stay open six weeks longer than before, through April 30, thanks to donations and a state grant, with 60 beds, breakfast and dinner, pet-friendly space and a new separate area for families. Executive director Heather Crockett said shelter demand rose 34% last winter despite it being the warmest on record, which she attributes largely to the economy, and the center needs 63 volunteers a week. item.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump administration push to set aside thousands of California ballots
item.description:
On the eve of the final day of midterm voting, the Supreme Court, with no public dissents, refused the Trump administration's request that California set aside mail ballots in a case involving 20,000 people it flagged as likely noncitizens, a list state officials said was filled with errors. Lower courts had sided with California, and the same day Chief Judge James Boasberg ruled that the administration's last-minute demands on state election officials likely violated the Constitution's Elections Clause. In a separate hearing, a Justice Department attorney agreed that a high error rate was "a fair statement," and California Attorney General Rob Bonta said the appeal "reeks of desperation."

item.title: 2 amendments, 1 fight: What's on Utah's ballot this November
item.description:
Utah voters will decide two constitutional amendments: Amendment A, which passed the Legislature without opposition, would replace the requirement to publish proposed amendments in newspapers in every county for two months with a method lawmakers choose at least 60 days before the vote, fixing the rule that voided Amendment D in 2024. Amendment B, sponsored by Sen. Lincoln Fillmore, would require 60% approval for citizen initiatives that create or raise taxes, which Fillmore framed as asking "How easy do you want it to be to raise taxes on your neighbors?" Opponents, including the Vote No campaign led by Elizabeth Rasmussen, call it a power grab; the 2018 Medicaid expansion passed with 53.3% and would have failed under the rule, while a September poll found 50% support and 21% opposition.

item.title: Parents of 1-year-old fatally shot by police protest at Mississippi Attorney General's Office
item.description:
The parents of Kohen Wiley, a 1-year-old killed in June when Senatobia police Sgt. Hunter Foster fired into a moving car outside a Walmart during a shoplifting call, led a protest Monday at the office of Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch, which ruled last month that the shooting was justified. Body camera footage shows the car reversing into another vehicle and then accelerating toward Foster, who fired through the front passenger window where Kohen sat on his mother's lap; Foster's attorney says he had "no choice." Kohen's father, Davion Williams, said he wants Foster prosecuted and Fitch out of office, and the ATF is investigating a Saturday fire that damaged the Senatobia police building.

item.title: Rubio meets Venezuelan counterpart as US presses for progress on election preparations
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco in Washington on Monday, two weeks after Venezuela's interim authorities and opposition agreed on a blueprint for electoral reforms ahead of elections that could come in 2027. The State Department said they discussed reforms laying "the groundwork for free, fair, and credible elections," and Rubio urged the release of Venezuela's remaining political prisoners. The meeting was one of the highest-level contacts with acting President Delcy Rodríguez's government since a U.S. military raid in January captured Nicolás Maduro, who denies drug trafficking charges.

item.description:
Federal and local authorities announced Operation Deep Cover to increase law enforcement in Dallas' Deep Ellum entertainment district, where three shootings early Sunday killed four people and wounded 15 within about an hour and 15 minutes. Halloween-weekend mass shootings killed at least eight people nationwide, including at a Jackson, Mississippi, nightclub costume party, outside Birmingham's Legion Field after the Magic City Classic and in a Bloomington, Indiana, nightlife area. item.description:
Lori Vallow Daybell's attorney Craig Durham asked the Idaho Supreme Court on Monday for a new trial, arguing she was denied her counsel of choice when the trial judge disqualified attorney Mark Means over his representation of her husband, Chad Daybell, a ruling Durham called "unconstitutional." Assistant Attorney General Jeff Nye countered that Means had served as Chad Daybell's attorney and kept filing inappropriate documents while Lori Daybell was deemed incompetent, saying "Nothing that happened here is normal, but that doesn't mean there was error in any of it." Asked whether a reversal could reopen the death penalty, Durham said his client is aware of the risks, and the court will rule later on her appeal of the 2023 convictions in the deaths of JJ Vallow, Tylee Ryan and Tammy Daybell.

item.title: A mystery skeleton found in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally have an identity
item.description:
The man buried in a fourth-century Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey, inscribed to "Valerius Amandinus," was likely a late Anglo-Saxon abbot, most probably Ælfwig, abbot from A.D. 993 to around 1020, according to a study by abbey consultant archaeologist Warwick Rodwell published Oct. 20. Radiocarbon dating placed the man, who died between 35 and 49, between A.D. 987 and 1052, and traces of a lime-packed timber coffin inside plus an Anglo-Saxon cross on the lid pointed to a high-status burial. Rodwell said the reuse was likely an honor because stone coffins had become scarce, and "Acquiring a secondhand stone coffin was considered a 'prize.'"

Charging documents say a skeletal survey of their 2-month-old daughter, brought to a hospital July 29 because she wasn't moving her arm, found multiple fractures in various stages of healing, including in her ribs, wrist, hands and feet, which doctors determined were "all non-accidental." Olivia Whiteley of Reliable Refuge noted net international migration fell from 2.7 million in 2024 to 1.3 million in 2025 and is expected to drop to about 321,000 in 2026, even though it drove nearly 21% of Utah's 2024-25 population growth. She said Utah, long able to resettle more than 1,000 refugees a year, welcomed only 152 this year, and urged Congress to codify a refugee floor shaped by state input.

Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill, seeking a fifth term against Republican Kent Davis, gave a July presentation to the Major County Prosecutors Council on charging ICE agents who violate state law, saying "ICE does not get to violate rights of our citizens." Utah ICE arrests hit a record 613 in June, and Gill, who says he does not seek to obstruct deportations, fears surging enforcement leaves immigrant residents afraid to report crimes. Davis, Gill's former deputy, says the DA has no role in civil immigration enforcement and points to a December 2025 legislative audit finding that about half of declined felony cases lacked detailed explanations and that diversion programs don't track recidivism, while Gill cites county crime at a decade low.

item.description:
A Yakima County, Washington, resident with underlying health conditions who caught bird flu from infected dairy cows died Nov. 1, the first U.S. bird flu death of 2026 and the third since the virus entered dairy cattle in February 2024. County officials are monitoring the person's contacts, and a third Washington case, also tied to infected cows, has mild symptoms; the state has reported 33 infected dairy herds since Oct. 8. No human-to-human spread has been documented in the U.S., and health officials say the risk to the public remains low.

A Russian Telegram channel said a group called Hitcore claimed the Ukrainian breach, which could not be verified, and Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said state agencies face constant cyberattacks, a growing number of them using AI. item.title: 'Oil pulling': Natural, stronger mouthwash or waste of time?
item.description:
Dentists say oil pulling, the Ayurvedic practice of swishing coconut or another edible oil for up to 20 minutes that has resurfaced on social media, adds little to brushing and flossing; a 2022 meta-analysis found lower bacterial counts but limited evidence of less plaque or gum inflammation. Dr. Matthew Messina, a consumer advisor for the American Dental Association, said there is no evidence it helps or harms, and San Diego-area dentist Dr. Kami Hoss said it offers a "false sense of protection." Oil pulling is no substitute for antibiotics for a gum infection, and Messina said mouthwash, unlike oil, has antibacterial and fluoride benefits but should still only supplement brushing.

item.title: Anthropic says you can't be mean to Claude. It's not about feelings
item.description:
Anthropic's October update to its usage policy bars users from engaging in "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" toward its Claude models and could lead to permanent bans in extreme cases, though a spokesperson told CNN that Claude ending conversations remains the main enforcement tool and that frustration, blunt feedback and research are not targeted. The rule drew mockery, including a melting-face emoji from Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman, but experts say it reflects more than concern for a machine's feelings. Former Reddit CEO Yishan Wong argued abusive inputs could end up in training data, and William and Mary professor Jindong Wang said research shows prompt tone can affect AI performance without implying emotion.

item.title: Russia's security service detains a teenager planning a 'terror attack' after a US tip-off
item.description:
Russia's FSB said it detained a teenage Russian citizen suspected of planning an attack on Moscow's Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve after U.S. law enforcement shared information, a day after the U.S. Embassy warned of a "credible threat of a mass casualty event" there. According to the FSB, the suspect followed a neo-Nazi Telegram channel and posted TikTok photos of himself in tactical gear with an apparent weapon and of the museum captioned "I found a place," and airsoft weapons were found at his home. The agency thanked the U.S., a contrast with Vladimir Putin's dismissal of a 2024 U.S. warning days before the Crocus City Hall attack killed more than 140 people.

item.title: 81 years later, a son pays tribute to his father's WWII mercy ride
item.description:
In early September, 56-year-old Greg Hoole rented a heavy town bike and rode 175 kilometers from Amsterdam to Assen over two days, retracing the trip his father, Hank, made at 14 on a bicycle with metal rims in the spring of 1945 after carrying food to his own father in Nazi-occupied Amsterdam. Greg found the story while rereading his late father's autobiography, which he had helped write and edit, and said he spent the ride wishing he had asked questions such as "How did you know where to go?" Unlike his father, he had rubber tires, a bike path the whole way and Apple Maps, and at the finish he said "I felt like I was on top of the world."

item.title: A drone motor in a garage. Natural gas to jet fuel. A power grid under pressure. What Utah builders made in days
item.description:
At the Hard Tech Hackathon during Utah Hard Tech Week, builders had about two days to turn ideas in energy, AI infrastructure, defense and aerospace into working prototypes, and Rogue Technologies co-founders Nate Roberts and Peter Hartvigsen won the Nucleus challenge's $10,000 bounty with a custom AI model that ran 51 times faster than conventional simulations of a reactor turning natural gas into jet fuel. Other entries included Joe Blash's garage-built machine for winding drone-motor coils, a first step toward U.S.-made drone motors, Juan Lizarazo's DETOUR software for timing business energy storage around grid prices, and an AI-to-3D-printing site called Printerest. State entrepreneurship official Tyler Jennings said Utah favors hackathons over pitch contests because "anybody can tell a story," describing the state's culture as one of "scrappy builders."

item.title: Churches celebrate All Saints' Day after Halloween
item.description:
Several Salt Lake-area churches marked All Saints' Day on Sunday, including First United Methodist, where Pastor Kelsie Parrish planned to read the names of community members lost over the past year during Holy Communion, and the Cathedral of the Madeleine, whose choir was scheduled to sing works by Victoria and Britten. Rev. Dr. Hank Malone of St. John's Lutheran Church described the preceding Halloween as a way to mock the devil, since Christ has taken away death's sting. Parrish said simultaneous observances worldwide remind believers "we are the body of Christ," and a diocesan Mass at Mount Calvary Catholic Cemetery was set for All Souls' Day on Monday.

item.title: What new earnings data reveals about Utah's college grads vs. Utah's high school grads
item.description:
Utah ranks No. 2 nationally, behind only Delaware, for how much its college credential holders out-earn high school graduates, according to HEA Group analysis of federal College Scorecard data: four years after finishing, alums typically earn $74,202 versus $37,112 for Utahns with only a diploma. Utah bachelor's graduates in computer and information technology administration ranked first in the nation on the earnings premium at $127,178, while the state's cosmetology graduates typically earn $9,000 less than high school graduates. The gap carries new stakes under a Department of Education framework that will cut federal loan eligibility for programs whose graduates repeatedly fail to out-earn diploma holders, which Under Secretary Nicholas Kent said ensures taxpayers back only programs that leave graduates "financially better off."

item.title: Does your life have meaning? Start by answering these 2 questions
item.description:
Accepting the Sutherland Institute's George A. Sutherland Award, Harvard business professor and author Arthur Brooks described happiness as a balance of enjoyment, satisfaction and meaning, and said half of his students can no longer answer his two-question exam on why they are alive and what they would give their lives for. Brooks blamed smartphones for the decline since 2008, saying his students "have eradicated every moment of boredom from their lives — and their lives are boring." He praised Utah as a model, saying that if America were more like it, "we'd have a lot fewer problems," and the institute gave its Family Values Award to former Gov. Mike Leavitt and Jacalyn Leavitt.

item.title: Mother-daughter duo creates pirate Halloween displays
item.description:
Staci Gifford of Eagle Mountain and her daughter, Kailee Burdette of Saratoga Springs, have built Pirates of the Caribbean-themed Halloween yards every year since 2018, Pirates of Thunder Gulch and Pirates of Utah Lake, adding homemade props and animatronics that come alive after dark. Burdette's social media posts now draw visitors from well beyond the neighborhood, who hunt for hidden Mickeys to earn a treasure and get homemade Disney churros and popcorn. Gifford, whose decorating began with three scarecrows dressed in her kids' clothes, said the point is family time, calling Halloween "a really fun time for families to grow close."

item.title: Nonprofit temporarily closes its doors, impacting more than 20,000
item.description:
Community Action Services and Food Bank, a Provo nonprofit founded in 1967 that served more than 24,000 people last year in Utah, Wasatch and Summit counties, closed until further notice Sunday while its board weighs next steps, after an effort to raise $1.5 million to stay open into next year. Utah County Commissioner Skyler Beltran called the closure a travesty and blamed what he called "financial and operational mismanagement" rather than any lack of government support, saying the county is working to protect the roughly 20,000 people who rely on its services. The county has taken over the warming center, which was scheduled to open Nov. 1 as planned, and CEO Caitlin Rangel said the need for the services "has not gone away."

item.title: Family identifies Ogden Canyon crash victim, prepares to say goodbye
item.description:
In a statement released on Halloween, the 14th anniversary of her adoption at age 7, the family of 22-year-old Katie Sue Ruth Huggins said she is on life support and not expected to survive, and that as an organ donor her gift will "carry her love forward." The family remembered her love of motorcycles, animals, family and friends and asked for privacy. She was critically injured Oct. 27 when her motorcycle collided at the mouth of Ogden Canyon with a vehicle authorities confirmed was driven by Box Elder County Sheriff Kevin Potter, who is now on voluntary administrative leave.

item.title: Longtime homeless cleanup nonprofit shuts down, leaving 125 unemployed
item.description:
Advantage Services, a Utah social enterprise founded in 1992 that employed about 125 people, most of them experiencing homelessness or other hardships, ceased operations Saturday after the state Office of Homeless Services declined CEO Rob Ferris' request for emergency bridge funding. Its troubles deepened when its largest contract, with Salt Lake City's Urban Services Division, was cut roughly in half from about $2 million, and Ferris had furloughed about 110 workers earlier this month after missing payroll; he now plans to sell assets, including the vehicle fleet, to pay out unused vacation as severance. Former office manager Megan Belagam said she feels betrayed and that the shutdown "has dehumanized" the workers.

item.title: Race for Campus Safety draws record turnout as awareness of relationship violence grows
item.description:
More than 800 people took part in Saturday's Race for Campus Safety at the University of Utah, up from about 100 at the 2022 inaugural event honoring Lauren McCluskey, a student killed on campus by her ex-boyfriend in 2018. Her mother, Jill McCluskey, credited students' growing awareness of relationship violence and said safeguards the university now has, such as parole checks, lethality assessments and victim advocates, "would have made a difference." Proceeds will help the Lauren McCluskey Foundation expand programs nationwide, including Lauren's Promise, a pledge to listen to and believe people facing threats that faculty at 480 universities have taken.

item.title: St. George woman donates wind phone to help individuals 'talk' to loved ones lost
item.description:
A phone-booth-style wind phone, where visitors can dial a number that reminds them of someone who has died and say what they never got to, now stands beside a bench at St. George's Tonaquint Nature Center near the Rainbow Bridge pet memorial. Shaelynn Del Toro, 23, created it after her uncle died unexpectedly in August 2025 without a chance to say goodbye, hand-painting the box with butterflies and a rainbow and adding the 988 crisis number and a QR code. City parks official Ben Neumann steered the project away from a park to the quieter spot, saying visitors can simply sit and "let your words go in the wind," an idea that traces to a Japanese garden designer in 2010.

item.title: Republicans on defense in Texas while Democrats in Michigan can't get on the same page
item.description:
Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico made closing pitches Saturday in a tossup Texas Senate race that has become a gauge of frustration with President Donald Trump, with Talarico casting Paxton as corrupt and his fight against Elon Musk, who has spent more than $150 million to help Paxton, as "David vs. Goliath," while Paxton called Talarico too liberal for Texas. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed tried to quiet talk of friction with primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens in his competitive open-seat race against Republican Mike Rogers, a seat Democrats can ill afford to lose. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate edge, early ballots were nearing 50 million, and Trump campaigned by phone Saturday before planned Sunday rallies in Iowa and Kansas.

item.title: Man sentenced for assault, attempted kidnapping of woman who said he wanted to 'mark her'
item.description:
Arnold Nelson, 54, of West Jordan, will serve a year in jail and three years of probation after pleading guilty to aggravated assault and a reduced attempted aggravated kidnapping charge over a June attack in which a witness said he beat the woman he lived with using a stick and a hammer or tomahawk knife. According to a police affidavit, he had ordered her into the backyard so he could "mark her," and officers found her covered in blood. Judge Dianna Gibson suspended a prison term of up to five years but ordered addiction treatment and denied good-time credit.

item.title: Weber State students press to resurrect centers geared to Latino, Black and other students
item.description:
Weber State seniors Nick Eckstrom, Evan Burnett and Kolby Ferrell have started a petition and met with President Chris Mallett seeking to revive the cultural centers for Black, Latino, LGBTQ and other students that the university closed in 2024 after HB261 required dismantling DEI programming. Burnett said Mallett was open to the idea but raised questions about logistics and legality, and state guidance allows such centers only if they focus on cultural awareness, are open to all students and win Board of Higher Education approval. A university spokeswoman said closing the centers was a choice to customize support rather than a legal mandate, while Eckstrom rejected the law's premise, saying the centers "are about inclusion not exclusion."

item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that the Trump administration "didn't facilitate anything" in defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro's arrival in Miami, saying Bolsonaro had previously held a visa and Trump decided to let him in. Bolsonaro, who has refused to concede to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and declared himself the "true president-elect of Brazil," is under investigation at home for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion and had been ordered to surrender his passport.

item.title: Don't give up on buying your first home, Utahns advised
item.description:
A study commissioned by the Salt Lake Board of Realtors found 50.1% of Utah households headed by 25- to 34-year-olds owned their homes in 2024, well above the 40.4% national rate, which board president Scott Colemere partly credits to young Utahns being better at "adulting." Colemere argues buyers who save at least $15,000, shore up their credit and consider condos or townhomes can still get in, as 37-year-old Michael Peterson did in Herriman, even though a Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute report puts homeownership out of reach for about 91% of renters. State housing coordinator Steve Waldrip praised young buyers' resilience but warned "the headwinds are getting tougher," with Gov. Spencer Cox's goal of 35,000 starter homes by 2028 only about a quarter met.

item.title: Virginia, DC sue over Trump's arch, adding to legal challenges
item.description:
Washington, D.C., and Virginia sued Saturday to stop President Donald Trump's planned 250-foot memorial arch near the bridge to Arlington National Cemetery, arguing that three years of construction would snarl traffic, pollute the Potomac and hamper emergency response. It is the third lawsuit against the project, which the administration hopes to approve as soon as Thursday and possibly start building the same day, while Judge Tanya Chutkan weighs halting it and asked what harm a delay would cause "apart from the executive's desire to bedazzle the city." A 106-page plan filed Friday envisions a winged bronze Lady Liberty, an observation deck and offices, and officials say the arch will also serve a national security function.

item.description:
Salt Lake County offered in-person voting on a Saturday for the first time, letting residents cast ballots at the county government center on Halloween before trick-or-treating in the county's final early-voting window. County Clerk Lannie Chapman said voters can still use 29 drop boxes or vote in person starting at 7 a.m. Tuesday, with ballots due by 8 p.m., and that unregistered Utahns may register on Election Day, though those ballots stay provisional until eligibility is verified.

item.description:
U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed with prejudice Donald Trump's $10 billion defamation suit against The Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over its report on a sexually suggestive birthday letter bearing Trump's name in a 2003 album for Jeffrey Epstein, saying the president was "grasping at straws." Citing New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, Gayles ruled that the amended complaint, filed after he first dismissed the case in April, still failed to plead actual malice, and he noted the story had reported Trump's denial.

item.description:
A shooting inside a Spirit Halloween store at Fairfield, California's Solano Town Center on Friday night killed Constance Hages, 31, whom family members said was pregnant, and wounded six others, three of whom remained in critical condition Saturday. Police said the shooting appears to have been a targeted incident involving one suspect, detectives are still working to identify the person responsible, and the FBI sent an evidence response team. The mall canceled its Saturday trick-or-treating event, and the store will stay closed.

item.title: Rick Ross no longer faces felony charge in Miami Beach domestic violence case
item.description:
Miami prosecutors declined to file a felony battery-by-strangulation charge against rapper Rick Ross, citing insufficient evidence, and instead charged him with one misdemeanor count of domestic violence battery. A woman told police Ross slapped and struck her and restricted her breathing by grabbing her hoodie collar during an Aug. 28 dispute over an Instagram photo at his Star Island home, allegations he calls fabricated. His attorney, Bradley Horenstein, said her injury photos showed no sign of strangulation and asked the public to "wait for it all to play out in court."

Alaska's Republican-led state government asked a federal judge Saturday to dismiss a Justice Department lawsuit, filed at President Donald Trump's direction, that seeks to block certification of a possible win by Democrat Mary Peltola in the U.S. Senate race because a second candidate named Dan Sullivan is on the ballot. The state called a new request to segregate ballots cast for that Sullivan "both disturbing and impossible" without violating voter privacy, noting the incumbent is listed as a Republican while the other appears simply as Daniel J. Sullivan. Trump has also called for Peltola's prosecution after The New York Times reported that Democrats' campaign appeared to have helped recruit the second Sullivan.

item.title: Former church building in Rush Valley prepares to reopen as museum
item.description:
Volunteers have logged more than 4,000 hours over five years restoring Rush Valley's 1907 Clover Ward meetinghouse, which had been converted to house the town's fire truck, and it will be dedicated as a museum on April 28, 120 years to the day after its original dedication. That date was set only after project manager John Cluff, following five years of fruitless archive searches, obtained a handwritten program from the Church History Library confirming that then-Elder Heber J. Grant performed the first dedication. Donated and discounted work worth more than $200,000 cost the project $90,000, and Carol Cluff said she hopes the building becomes "an asset to the whole county."

item.title: Advisories issued as more rain, snow return to Utah, including areas recovering from floods
item.description:
An atmospheric river colliding with a cold front is expected to bring heavy mountain snow and valley rain to Utah from late Halloween night into Monday, prompting a National Weather Service winter weather advisory and flood watches. Areas above 10,000 feet in the Cottonwood Canyons and Uintas could get 18 to 24 inches, one model gives Alta a 40% chance of at least 18 inches, and forecasters raised parts of southwest Utah and the Four Corners to a moderate flood risk. Grand Junction hydrologist Erin Walter said her office is most worried about the Four Corners area that flooded last week, where some San Juan County families still cannot return home.

item.title: New study casts doubt on theory about the role comets played in kick-starting life on Earth
item.description:
Computer simulations published in Scientific Reports suggest comets striking the early Earth were moving too fast to deliver intact hydrogen cyanide, a key prebiotic ingredient, undercutting a theory dating to at least 1961 that they seeded the building blocks of life. Across 100,000 runs, lead author Richard Anslow found that on average there were "no successful impacts," and rare fluke hits would have needed to land where liquid water and other necessary chemicals were already present, though slower impacts on ancient Mars may have preserved more of the compound. Outside scientists Queenie Chan and Nicolle Zellner weren't ready to rule comets out, with Chan noting the chemical may have formed sturdier compounds before the comets ever reached Earth.

item.title: From salmonberry harvests to traditional tattoos, Native American culture is November spotlight
item.description:
For Native American Heritage Month, an AP collection of short profiles highlights joy in Indigenous communities, opening with Las Vegas Paiute artist Fawn Douglas, whose new Wai Gallery shows Indigenous art meant to dismantle the stereotype that Native people are a monolith. Other vignettes follow a Kipnuk, Alaska, family back to pick salmonberries a year after Typhoon Halong, Pascua Yaqui foster mother Rosa Soto Alvarez's advocacy for the Indian Child Welfare Act, and the NAIWA Daughters, Indigenous girls whose resolution led the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians to recognize a river system's rights. The collection also visits a Minneapolis Ojibwe and Dakota language program's sugarbush outing, a Tulsa effort to replace a lost Indian youth center, and tattoo artist Hodokii Johnson's work restoring ancestral markings.

item.title: 'A bucket-list hike': Summiting Mount Timpanogos beyond peak season
item.description:
Utah County hiker Josh Abbott recently summited Mount Timpanogos, nearly 12,000 feet up, in late-fall snow and ice, climbing with experienced guides and carrying spikes, axes and ropes. Juggling a full-time job and full-time school, Abbott said the mountains offer "just a pause" from both, a love of exploring he traces to childhood outings his mother allowed as long as he checked in by two-way radio. He has also climbed Guatemala's Acatenango volcano but says much of the reward lies close to home and in the journey rather than the summit.

item.title: Elderly couple loses life savings to scammer posing as FBI agent
item.description:
Gail Walsh of Burbank, Illinois, says she and her husband lost $18,400, nearly everything they had, after an Aug. 15 caller posing as an FBI investigator, who already knew her account balances, talked her through withdrawing the cash and handing it to a man in a black SUV outside a second Chase branch. The caller claimed some bills were counterfeit and promised a bank employee would bring out "genuine cash," but no one came, and Walsh said Chase told her it could do nothing. The FBI says such impersonation scams are rising and warns against giving money or personal information to anyone who initiated contact.

item.description:
Small Business Administration official Lisa Shimkat traveled from Washington to tour La Casa Del Tamal's Post District location in Salt Lake City, which Mexican immigrant Cristina Olvera opened last year with an SBA-backed loan after two decades of selling homemade tamales. The business took off from a 2019 food court stand at West Valley City's Azteca Swapmeet after daughter Frida's social media push drew local foodies, and Olvera's five children and son-in-law Andres Sanchez, CEO of the parent LCDT Restaurant Group, now run key parts of it. item.title: Rising health costs and coverage changes are big concerns for older adults as Election Day nears
item.description:
Healthcare costs are a top worry for older voters heading into Tuesday's midterms, with an AARP poll finding 83% of voters over 50 extremely motivated to vote as Medicare enrollees weigh higher Part D caps, expiring premium subsidies and Advantage plan pullbacks taking effect in 2027. Ohio retiree Barbara Weigand, 83, who withdrew $4,000 from retirement savings for cancer care, said she has considered taking medication every other day, and about 1 in 5 people in a KFF survey reported cutting pills or skipping doses over cost. AARP also found family caregivers now spend an average of $11,508 a year, up from $7,242 in 2021, while Social Security's trust funds face a 2034 shortfall.

As Utah fights prediction market Kalshi in court over what the state calls illegal gambling, Utah marriage and family therapist Gregory Noel says DraftKings CEO Jason Robins' advice to talk with kids about gambling addiction falls short because "the internet is a lawless game." Salt Lake City planning commissioners pushed back on Intermountain Health's plan to move LDS Hospital from the Avenues to the former Sears Block near 754 S. State, chiefly because it puts about 190 feet of ground-floor retail in an offsite parking structure instead of the hospital, which several questioned against the development agreement's call for ground-floor activation. HDR Architects' Eric Meub said limiting entrances keeps the secured hospital safe, calling the issue "truly life and death," but commissioner Richard Leverett worried the result could look like a correctional facility, and Landon Kracsek floated retail beside the hospital with no interior connection. Commissioner Aimee Burrows also objected to a requested allowance for EIFS cladding, and elements such as a Main Street skybridge still need City Council approval ahead of a hoped-for groundbreaking by year's end.

item.title: Utah 5-year-old with Down syndrome walks Messi on the field, scores goals with Beckham
item.description:
Five-year-old Huddy Droubay of Syracuse, who has Down syndrome, walked onto the field with Lionel Messi and scored goals with David Beckham at an Inter Miami game after Beckham noticed a viral video of him beaming through a city-league soccer game. The connection grew into signed jerseys and a letter inviting the family to Miami, where Beckham wore a jersey printed with Huddy's affectionate nickname for him. His mom, Melanie Droubay, said she wants him to grow up knowing "he belongs everywhere."

item.title: Online registry highlights Utah's haunted 'real estate'
item.description:
Real estate broker Kris Bowen created Utah's Real Haunted Houses: The Registry, which lists 42 locations and their ghost stories, after years of buyers asking whether a home was haunted or someone had died there. He said sellers don't have to disclose stigmatized properties but can't lie if asked, and his team researched entries through state archives, property records and old newspapers. A favorite is the Capitol Theatre, where staff say a 17-year-old usher who died fighting a 1949 basement fire still controls the lights.

item.title: Utah to start enforcing its law requiring porn sites to verify ages of users
item.description:
Utah's Department of Commerce will begin enforcing its age-verification law for adult websites on Monday, saying a court order that paused SB73's provision targeting VPN workarounds still leaves it free to investigate sites and fine them up to $2,500 per violation. The law, sponsored by Sen. Calvin Musselman, also taxes adult sites to fund enforcement and youth mental health, and commerce director Margaret Busse said the state is using "advanced technology" to check compliance and is not after fine revenue. Aylo, the Pornhub owner suing over the VPN provision, said enforcement "changes nothing about our operations" and argued age checks belong on the device.

item.title: Halloween through the years: A look back at Utah's spooky season traditions
item.description:
KSL dug through its archives for a look at decades of Utah Halloweens, from a 1990 couple who married dressed as Frankenstein and his bride to 1988 yards turned into mock graveyards and a cemetery worried about vandalism in 1991. Safety advice recurs, with 1983 warnings about unsealed candy and a Holladay bank asking customers to skip costumes that resembled robbers, while Operation Desert Storm costumes turned up in 1991. Even complaints about stores pushing Christmas before Halloween date back to a 1995 report.

item.title: Red Cross urges Utahns to check smoke alarms as daylight saving time ends
item.description:
With daylight saving time ending Sunday, the American Red Cross is urging Utahns to test smoke alarms, since home fires rise about 20% nationwide in November and December as cooking and heating increase, said Jeremiah Lafranca of the Greater Salt Lake Chapter. Red Cross volunteers have answered about 140 Utah home fires so far this year. The group recommends monthly tests and replacing alarms after 10 years, and offers free installation of up to three alarms per home, including bed shakers for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

item.title: Pamela Atkinson remembered: 'A living embodiment' of Christlike love
item.description:
Hundreds of Utahns of many faiths gathered at First Presbyterian Church to remember Pamela Atkinson, the homeless and refugee advocate known as "Utah's Mother Teresa," who died Oct. 10 at 93. The Rev. Jamie White said Psalm 23 was the last thing he heard her say, and eulogists including Gov. Spencer Cox, Sharon Eubank and Elder Patrick Kearon tied her work founding clinics, advising officials and organizing aid to her faith, with Cox recalling her final message: "Just follow Jesus." White also delivered a message she had asked him to share, encouraging people to reach out and help others.

item.description:
Single mom Kenzie Bates went from throwing family birthday parties while working several jobs to running an events business whose clients include a luxury handbag store's grand opening and stars of Real Housewives of Salt Lake City and Secret Lives of Mormon Wives. She landed early high-profile clients partly by discounting events in exchange for photos she could share on social media. Bates said the work took a lot of sacrifice, and that her goal is for guests to feel a "VIP experience."

item.title: FTC orders Walmart, Delta and others to share how they use personal data to set prices and pay
item.description:
The Federal Trade Commission has ordered Delta, United, JetBlue, Walmart, Target, Lyft, DoorDash and Instacart to explain whether they use personal data such as loyalty-program activity to vary prices between customers, and whether gig drivers' pay is set using data like their phone usage or ride-acceptance history. Chairman Andrew Ferguson said the agency intends to scrutinize "opaque methodology" in these industries, and it says it can go to federal court if companies don't comply. Several companies denied the practice, with Delta citing "zero tolerance for discriminatory or predatory pricing," while the FTC weighs a separate proposal requiring disclosure of personalized pricing, open for comment until Nov. 21.

item.description:
Daybreak families can plan trick-or-treat routes using an online map at DaybreakHolidays.com and PorchlightVillage.com and the Porchlight app, where more than 160 homes have registered their Halloween displays, up from about 75 when organizer Mallory Curnow started. Some participants hire actors or DJs, and the owner of a Stranger Things-themed house said the map helps visitors find smaller displays between the big ones. Curnow said getting on the map brings more trick-or-treaters to a street.

item.title: Las Vegas children's hospital groundbreaking brings hope to southern Utah family
item.description:
Intermountain Health broke ground this week in Las Vegas on Nevada's first standalone children's hospital, expected to open in 2030 with pediatric cancer, cardiac and emergency care that Desert Region president Mitch Cloward said will also serve southern Utah kids. For St. George's Stone family, whose son Nash was born at 27 weeks, spent 478 days in NICUs and still depends on a ventilator and feeding tube, trips to Primary Children's in Salt Lake City mean packing what they call "an ICU on wheels." A two-hour drive to Las Vegas, mom Lindee Stone said, would make specialist visits "just a day trip."

item.title: Judge puts off decision in Comey case as prosecutors pursue new indictment
item.description:
U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden declined for now to dismiss a placeholder criminal information filed against former FBI Director James Comey over a 2016 leak tied to a New York Times story on a secret Yahoo email-scanning order, giving prosecutors time to seek a grand jury indictment. Comey's lawyers argue the 10-year statute of limitations required an indictment, not an information he never agreed to, and that leaving the case open is "very unfair and unjust." The judge, noting grand juries in Washington have rejected politically delicate cases, quipped that ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days and warned against any "dawn raid" to arrest Comey.

item.title: Fear struck Utah: Retired KSL reporter recalls beginning of Ted Bundy saga
item.description:
Retired KSL-TV reporter Lynn Packer recounts how, in October 1974, Midvale's police chief came to the station to report his 17-year-old daughter Melissa Smith missing, unknowingly giving Utah its first local coverage of Ted Bundy's crimes. Drawing on KSL archives and records gathered with researcher Tiffany Jean, the piece traces Bundy's arrival in Salt Lake City that September through the killings of Smith, Laura Aime and Debra Kent, the failed abduction of Carol DaRonch, and his 1975 trips to Colorado and Idaho. "Fear sort of struck the state," Packer said, adding that it was "more by luck" that police finally found a suspect when a trooper stopped Bundy's Volkswagen in Granger in August 1975.

item.title: Amendment B fight attracts big money ahead of Election Day
item.description:
Utah's Amendment B, which would require tax-raising citizen initiatives to win at least 60% of the vote, has drawn more than $3 million in opposition spending from Utahns Protecting Our Constitution, much of it from out-of-state donors, while supporters have raised far less. Taxpayer Shield PAC's Rusty Cannon said that money shows opponents "want to be able to raise your taxes easily," while opposition spokesperson Scott Cuthbertson argued voters should need only the same simple majority the Legislature does. A Noble Predictive Insights poll found 56% of likely voters opposed and 34% in favor ahead of Tuesday's election.

item.title: AAA offers $10 Lyft credits for Halloween weekend
item.description:
AAA Utah is paying for $10 Lyft credits from Friday, Oct. 30, through Sunday, Nov. 1, redeemed by scanning QR codes posted at participating bars and restaurants, in a Halloween-weekend effort with the Utah Department of Public Safety and the Utah Restaurant Association. State crash data show alcohol-related crashes are 15 times more likely to be fatal, and impaired-driver crashes killed 102 people in Utah in 2025. With Halloween on a Saturday, Utah Highway Patrol Lt. Zach Randall said extra troopers will be out looking for impaired drivers.

The Tooele City Council is set to present Heart of Service awards Wednesday to 18 of 31 Tooele Valley residents recognized this year as part of the America250 service initiative, with JustServe volunteers Annalese and Cameron Thorpe helping gather nominations. Among the honorees is a Switchpoint Tooele food pantry volunteer who began serving twice a week after her husband died rather than grieve alone at home. item.description:
Steven Matthew Sattley, 52, of Washington City has been charged with burglary and theft after an August break-in at an Ivins home where silver bars and diamond jewelry valued at about $125,000 were taken. Police say family members noticed sudden spending on veneers, a vehicle and clothes that he attributed to a Family Dollar promotion, though he had never worked there, and his phone showed searches for silver pawn shops and an AI-drafted email offering $280,000 cash for a house. Cedar City parents Jarrid Anthony Stoklosa and Amelia Mae Ramirez, both 21, each face seven first-degree felony counts of aggravated child abuse after X-rays in March showed their 36-day-old son had seven fractures to his ribs, arm and leg in various stages of healing. item.title: Dockworkers worldwide strike against arms shipments and to demand better working conditions
item.description:
Dockworkers at more than 100 ports joined a Friday strike called by unions in France, Italy, Greece, Spain, Turkey and Morocco against weapons shipments and the "militarization of ports," as well as for better working conditions. Actions ranged from full-day stoppages at ports such as Le Havre, Marseille and Piraeus to demonstrations in Istanbul and Italian ports alongside a national general strike. Logistics experts expected limited effects on global trade, though perishable goods and already-congested ports like Genoa could see delays.

item.description:
A Farmington front yard filled entirely with carved pumpkins, rather than the usual ghouls and gravestones, is one of about 15 stops on a city pumpkin tour where visitors vote for favorites. item.title: Boston researchers discover differences in colon cancer tumor cells in younger patients
item.description:
Researchers at Mass General Brigham, Dana-Farber and the Broad Institute analyzed 189 colorectal tumors and more than 850,000 cell nuclei and found that tumors from patients under 50 contain a higher proportion of stromal cells, which can suppress immune response and block drugs, along with gene differences that may drive more aggressive disease. Senior co-author Dr. Ana Anderson said the work doesn't explain why young-onset cases are rising but gives researchers differences to "dig into further." Survivor Kristen Vincent, diagnosed with stage 3 cancer at 37 and now five years clear, urged younger adults not to ignore warning signs.

item.title: What to know about the $6.3B hack on Binance, likely the biggest-ever crypto theft
item.description:
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, says hackers took more than $6 billion from its hot wallets in what appears to be the biggest crypto theft on record, and it has set aside $6.34 billion of its own funds to cover users while roughly $3 billion has been frozen. Blockchain firms TRM and Chainalysis attribute the attack to TraderTraitor, the North Korean unit the FBI blamed for last year's $1.5 billion Bybit hack, with TRM saying most of the funds moved out "in about 20 minutes." Co-CEO Richard Teng said attackers used a "self-destruct mechanism" that complicates the investigation, and withdrawals remain suspended.

item.title: Wall Street drops to its worst day since June after the sell-off for tech stocks deepens
item.description:
The S&P 500 fell 1.8% Friday for its worst day since June, with the Nasdaq down 2.9% and the Dow down 1.1%, as worries that the AI frenzy had pushed tech prices too high deepened. Intel lost almost 29%, its worst day since 1974, after a weak profit forecast, and Amazon slid after disclosing $42.4 billion in negative free cash flow over 12 months on heavy AI-driven spending, a day after Alphabet's record drop on similar concerns. One portfolio manager said the AI trade is moving into the "'show me' phase," while Treasury yields eased and crypto stocks fell after the Binance hack.

Ogden police and the Weber Metro CRASH team say the investigation follows the same steps as any serious-injury crash and may take weeks. item.title: Christa Pike says she's in constant pain and blames her failed execution on 'incompetence'
item.description:
In her first public statement since surviving a Sept. 30 lethal injection, Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike said she is in constant pain, still struggles to speak, and blames the failure on "incompetence." Pike, 50, was sentenced for the 1995 killing of classmate Colleen Slemmer, and her lawyers say two doses of pentobarbital left her arms burned and blistered, with experts suspecting an IV problem. Gov. Bill Lee has ordered an investigation and paused another execution, but said he expects her sentence to stand unless courts decide otherwise.

item.title: Peptides could soon be easier to get in the United States. Here's what to know
item.description:
HHS has posted a draft policy, open for 14 days of comment, under which it would not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies that compound six popular wellness peptides such as BPC-157 and TB-500 for patients with a prescription, even though the substances are not FDA-approved. The department says the move will steer users away from an unregulated gray market of foreign research-use-only products, following a narrow July vote by an FDA compounding advisory committee. Pharmacy compounders and the American Peptide Association welcomed it, while the Partnership for Safe Medicines said the outcome "shreds any sense of credibility and transparency," and one industry figure warned users to expect "a very different bill at the pharmacy counter."

item.title: Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a US general election
item.description:
The Vatican confirmed that Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV cast a mail-in ballot in Will County, Illinois, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms, making him the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election. The press office said he believes in "the right and the duty of citizens" to take part in democratic processes, and records show he requested the ballot Oct. 3, days before lung cancer surgery, and has voted in most general elections since 2000 along with both Democratic and Republican primaries. The vote comes after a public clash with President Trump over Leo's criticism of the Iran war and immigration enforcement.
